- Weaknesses: The benchmark currently shows zero solves for difficulty 4–5 in the reported runs, limiting insight into the highest-risk kernel/runc exploitation regimes; the paper’s significance depends on continued updating and on how widely the scenarios generalize. Also, the benchmark focuses on “escape to VM host,” which is appropriate for safety, but may diverge from production containment stacks (microVMs, gVisor, hardened seccomp/AppArmor), limiting immediate external validity.

Originality:
- Strengths: A dedicated container-escape benchmark with nested-sandbox methodology and scenario suite appears novel within the paper’s positioning (distinct from broader cyber benches). The explicit treatment of shortcut prevention in an agentic setting and the compute allocation analyses (parallel vs sequential) are valuable.
- Weaknesses: Many individual scenarios are built from known misconfigurations/CVEs and public PoCs (as intended); the novelty is primarily in packaging, methodology, and measurement rather than new technical exploitation techniques.

Overall, this is a well-motivated benchmark paper with a thoughtful safety-aware harness and useful initial baselines, but it would benefit from tighter experimental control/reporting and stronger validity evidence (human baselines, robustness checks, and clearer handling of provider-default differences).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Provider defaults: What are the exact generation parameters actually used per model/provider (temperature, top-p, tool-call policies), and how sensitive are results to harmonizing these settings across providers?
2) Missing samples: The paper reports 760/810 completed runs. Which model×scenario×epoch cells are missing, and do conclusions (especially difficulty-3 comparisons and “version regression”) hold under a missingness analysis or with reruns?
3) Scenario fidelity: For each scenario, what concrete hardening controls are intentionally disabled/enabled (seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux, user namespaces, cgroup v1/v2, kernel configs)? This impacts how representative the scenarios are of common Docker/K8s sandbox setups.
4) Hint ablation: Please provide the full hint text per scenario (or a taxonomy of hint granularity). Are hints always of comparable specificity (class vs exact CVE vs step hints), and could that explain the differential gains between models?
5) Robustness to shortcutting: Beyond manual transcript inspection, do you have an automated method to verify that a success used the intended vulnerability class (e.g., detecting SSH to host, docker API use, modprobe_path overwrite), and what is the estimated false negative rate of shortcut detection?
review.limitations: yes. The paper includes a limitations section and an impact statement that address scope (motivated adversary with shell access; intentionally introduced weaknesses; limited agent architectures) and notes generalization caveats. One constructive improvement would be to more explicitly discuss dual-use risk from releasing scenario implementations/PoCs, and clarify what is public vs held-out, how the private test set will be governed/updated, and whether release includes mitigations/hardening guidance alongside exploits.

title: Improving Reconstruction of Representation Autoencoder

review.summary:
The paper studies representation autoencoders for latent diffusion models that use high-dimensional vision foundation model (VFM) features (e.g., DINOv3) as latents. It identifies a key failure mode: VFM semantic features omit low-level information (color/texture), yielding poor reconstructions when used directly as an encoder. The proposed LV-RAE addresses this by treating VFM features as a fixed “base manifold” and training a lightweight encoder to predict a residual (local-variation) signal conditioned on both the image patches and the frozen VFM features; the latent is formed as a LayerNorm of (VFM features + residual), with an explicit L2 alignment loss to keep latents close to the VFM features.

The paper further investigates why high-dimensional, information-rich latents can hurt generation: decoders become highly sensitive to latent perturbations, producing artifacts when decoding imperfectly generated latents. Using a toy manifold/off-manifold construction, it argues this arises from excessive decoder responses along off-manifold directions, which proliferate with dimension. To mitigate this, the paper (i) fine-tunes the decoder with stochastic latent noise (and an adversarial loss) to improve robustness, and (ii) injects controlled noise into generated latents at inference to suppress artifacts. Experiments on ImageNet-1K and COCO at 256×256 report strong reconstruction metrics and competitive class-conditional generation (FID/IS, plus DINO-based FDD).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The LV-RAE design is simple and well-motivated: freezing the VFM base and learning only the missing residual avoids the “moving target” issue the paper attributes to joint fine-tuning with competing reconstruction/alignment losses. The method is clearly specified (latent construction, initialization, losses). The decoder-robustness intervention is supported by an ablation showing dramatic degradation of the original decoder under small latent noise and improved robustness after noise-augmented fine-tuning.
- Weaknesses / concerns: (1) The core claim that fine-tuning a VFM encoder with reconstruction+alignment is unstable because the base manifold drifts is plausible but not rigorously established; the evidence is mostly training curves on losses and a performance comparison. (2) The inference-time “add noise to generated latent” step improves reported metrics, but it is a heuristic that trades detail for smoothness; the paper does not deeply characterize the fidelity-diversity trade-off beyond FID/FDD trends and some visuals. (3) The toy experiment supports the qualitative mechanism, but it is highly stylized; it does not connect quantitatively to real decoders (e.g., measuring Jacobian norms along estimated off-manifold directions).

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally clear, with intuitive figures (framework overview; perturbation artifacts; toy experiment visualization) and concrete architectural/training details in the appendix. The two-stage training (LV-RAE then robust decoder) and the separation of reconstruction vs generation issues are well organized.
- Weaknesses: Some terminology/metrics are introduced without enough intuition (e.g., “rFDD” appears in Table 1 without a clear definition in the main text; FDD is defined later). Also, the method relies on specific choices (using pre-LayerNorm VFM features; specific initialization tricks; GAN loss with adaptive weight) whose individual contributions are not fully disentangled.

Significance:
- Strengths: Improving reconstruction fidelity while retaining diffusion-friendly semantics is a practically important bottleneck for LDM scaling, and the paper reports a large reconstruction gain over compared tokenizers (notably versus prior representation autoencoders) at 256×256. The robustness analysis and decoder fine-tuning address a real issue when using higher-dimensional latents for generation.
- Weaknesses: The experimental scope is limited to 256×256 ImageNet/COCO and class-conditional generation; it is unclear whether the gains persist at higher resolutions, for text-to-image settings, or across more varied diffusion backbones/samplers. Also, the decoder-noise inference heuristic may complicate downstream use cases that require crisp details.

Originality:
- Strengths: The “fixed semantic base + learned residual local variations” formulation is a clean architectural reframing relative to direct VFM alignment/fine-tuning, and the paper explicitly targets the reconstruction gap while maintaining near-perfect semantic alignment (via CKNNA). The explicit focus on decoder sensitivity in high-dimensional semantic latents and the two-part mitigation (training-time robustness + inference-time smoothing) is a coherent contribution.
- Weaknesses: Elements resemble known patterns (residual learning; denoising/augmentation for robustness; noise injection at inference), so the novelty is more in the specific combination and diagnosis in the representation-autoencoder-for-diffusion context rather than a fundamentally new modeling paradigm.

Overall, I find the approach technically solid and well supported by reconstruction and generation experiments at the studied setting, with the main reservations being limited external validation (resolution/tasks) and incomplete mechanistic validation of the “off-manifold Jacobian” story in real models.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How sensitive are the main results (reconstruction and generation) to the alignment weight η in Eq. (5)? In particular, what is the Pareto curve between PSNR/LPIPS and CKNNA when sweeping η, and does the method still outperform baselines at matched semantic alignment?

2) For the decoder sensitivity hypothesis: can you provide measurements on real LV-RAE decoders (not the toy decoder), e.g., estimating local Jacobian norms or output variation along directions orthogonal to the data manifold (approximated via PCA/tangent space of latents)? This would strengthen the claimed mechanism.

3) In Table 3/5, LV-RAE improves FDD substantially but is slightly worse than VA-VAE on gFID in some settings. Do you observe systematic differences in sample sharpness/diversity? Please include qualitative comparisons at matched guidance/noise settings and discuss when LV-RAE helps most.

4) The inference-time latent noise injection (Eq. 11) is crucial. How robust is the optimal \bar{\sigma} across model sizes, sampling steps, and datasets? Can a single \bar{\sigma} be used reliably, or does it require per-model tuning?

5) The decoder fine-tuning uses an adversarial loss with DINO-S/8 and differentiable augmentations. How much does GAN fine-tuning contribute beyond noise-augmented reconstruction-only fine-tuning, especially for generation metrics (FID/FDD) rather than reconstruction metrics?
review.limitations: Partially. The paper includes a brief impact statement but does not meaningfully discuss limitations or potential negative societal impacts beyond saying it “inherits standard ethical considerations.” I suggest: (i) explicitly discussing the trade-off introduced by inference-time noise injection (possible loss of fine details / bias toward smoother textures), (ii) noting that results are limited to 256×256 class-conditional ImageNet and may not transfer to higher resolution or text-to-image, (iii) discussing computational/memory costs of high-dimensional latents (f16d768) and transformer autoencoder inference, and (iv) expanding societal-impact discussion to cover misuse of improved generative fidelity and dataset bias amplification, even if not unique to this method.

title: T3D: Few-Step Diffusion Language Models via Trajectory Self-Distillation with Direct Discriminative Optimization

review.summary:
The paper targets efficient inference for masked diffusion language models (specifically block diffusion SDAR) under aggressive step budgets (few diffusion steps per block / high tokens-per-step). It proposes T3D, a self-distillation method that trains a student model on teacher-generated roll-out trajectories (pairs of intermediate masked states x_t and final sequences x_0) produced under the intended decoding heuristic, aiming to reduce train–test mismatch of intermediate states and improve few-step decoding.

T3D introduces (1) trajectory self-distillation (on-policy supervision from teacher trajectories rather than random masking), (2) a trajectory-level Direct Discriminative Optimization (DDO) objective using an implicit likelihood-ratio discriminator versus a reference model to encourage mode-seeking (reverse-KL-like) distillation under multimodal posteriors, and (3) a path-consistency regularizer that reweights token losses by decoding order to reduce error propagation. The paper provides theoretical results connecting trajectory distillation to improved on-policy posterior matching and reduced conditional total correlation (factorization error). Experiments on SDAR-1.7B-Chat and SDAR-4B-Chat over GSM8K, MATH500, MBPP, and HumanEval show improved accuracy/efficiency tradeoffs under tight decoding budgets and reasonable preservation of full-step decoding quality.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The core idea—distilling on teacher rollouts that match the inference-time masking/decoding distribution—is well-motivated and clearly instantiated via Eq. (5). The method is simple (no extra data labels) and the ablations in Appendix D support that DDO + path weighting + random-token corruption each matter for stability/quality (e.g., Table 5 shows severe collapse without the regularizers; Tables 6–7 show DDO variants outperform Naive TD in few-step regimes).
- Weaknesses: Several theoretical statements rely on strong assumptions that are not empirically validated. In particular, Assumption 4.2/B.1 (margin matching p_\phi(x_t)=p_\theta(x_t)) is critical for Proposition 4.3 and subsequent decomposition arguments; but in practice p_\theta changes during finetuning and inference-time x_t distributions may drift. Likewise, Theorem 4.5/B.8 uses “ideal optimality” and log-convex hull assumptions; this makes the theory more explanatory than predictive.
- The DDO trajectory loss (Eq. 7) is somewhat under-specified from an implementation standpoint: it uses expectations inside a sigmoid of an expected log-likelihood ratio, which differs from a more standard sample-wise logistic objective. The paper later presents an upper bound (Eq. 23), but the exact estimator used in practice (number of samples from p_\phi(\cdot|x_t) and p_{\theta_{ref}}(\cdot|x_t), whether the expectation is approximated with a single sample, whether Jensen is applied) is not clearly stated in the main text.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well-structured: clear motivation (few-step degradation due to factorization and distribution shift), method components laid out cleanly, and key results are summarized in tables with consistent settings (TokPS, block size). Appendices provide algorithm pseudocode and ablations.
- Weaknesses: Some definitions are confusing/inconsistent: the paper defines J_\phi(x_0,x_t)=p_\phi(x_0)q(x_t|x_0) (Eq. 13) but trajectory distillation uses p_\phi(x_t)p_\phi(x_0|x_t) (Def. 4.1), and the relationship between these in the generative (not data) setting is easy to misread. Also, the “decode one token per step to get best performance” teacher procedure is specific; it would help to more explicitly map it to SDAR’s block decoding mechanics and how x_t is constructed for distillation (some of this appears in Sec. 5.1, but it remains intricate).

Significance:
- Strengths: Few-step decoding for diffusion LMs is an important practical problem; the reported gains under aggressive TokPS are substantial in multiple settings (e.g., Table 1 shows consistent improvements over baselines, and Table 3 suggests improved throughput/latency with competitive or better accuracy under dynamic decoding). Preserving full-step performance (Table 2) is also valuable if one wants a single model usable across budgets.
- Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to the SDAR family and to four benchmarks; it is unclear how broadly the method transfers to other DLLM parameterizations/decoding schemes. Also, some comparisons show SFT (with real data) is competitive or better in certain settings, and the paper’s narrative could better clarify when self-distillation is preferred (e.g., data availability vs. performance).

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of on-policy trajectory distillation with a discriminative likelihood-ratio objective (DDO) applied at the conditional/trajectory level is a novel integration in this context, and the path-consistency reweighting tailored to blockwise decoding is a reasonable additional contribution.
- Weaknesses: Each ingredient is incremental relative to existing themes (trajectory distillation/consistency-style rollouts; reverse-KL/mode-seeking via discriminative training; token reweighting), but the paper’s novelty lies mainly in their specific combination and adaptation to few-step masked diffusion LM decoding.

Overall, the method appears promising and empirically effective, but there are clarity gaps around the exact DDO estimator and some reliance on strong assumptions in the theory, which together slightly reduce technical confidence.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How exactly is Eq. (7) optimized in practice? Specifically: for each (x_t), how many samples are drawn from p_\phi(\cdot|x_t) and p_{\theta_{ref}}(\cdot|x_t), and do you compute the sigmoid on a per-sample log-ratio or on an average (as written)? Please provide the exact Monte Carlo estimator.
2) How do you sample from p_{\theta_{ref}}(x_0|x_t) for the “fake” term during training? Is it a single denoising step conditioned on x_t, a full rollout to x_0 under the reference policy, or something else?
3) Assumption 4.2 (p_\phi(x_t)=p_\theta(x_t)) is central to Proposition 4.3. Do you have empirical evidence that x_t marginals remain close during training, or can you quantify drift (e.g., via KL between masking patterns / state distributions) under your finetuning procedure?
4) The training trajectory dataset is collected under a specific teacher decoding procedure (block size 4, steps per block 4, low-confidence remasking + static decoding). If inference uses different heuristics (different thresholds, different remasking schedule, different block size), how sensitive is T3D to this mismatch? Do you have a cross-schedule generalization test?
5) Reproducibility/compute: how many total trajectory samples (or tokens) are used for distillation, and how does performance scale with dataset size and number of training steps?
review.limitations: No. The “Impact Statement” effectively says no societal consequences need highlighting, which is not an adequate limitations discussion. The paper should (a) discuss risks of amplifying model biases/toxicity through self-distillation on model-generated data, (b) note potential degradation of diversity/mode collapse given mode-seeking objectives, (c) clarify that gains are shown on limited benchmarks/models and may not generalize, and (d) report compute/data costs and environmental considerations of generating large trajectory datasets and finetuning.

title: Rethink Efficiency Side of Neural Combinatorial Solver: An Offline and Self-Play Paradigm

review.summary: The paper proposes ECO, an “offline self-play” training framework for neural combinatorial optimization on routing problems (TSP, CVRP) with an emphasis on efficiency. ECO uses a two-phase learning paradigm: (i) supervised fine-tuning (behavior cloning) from high-quality solver trajectories to warm start, followed by (ii) iterative Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) where preference pairs are created from multiple samples per instance (best vs worst), with periodic reference-model updates. To strengthen preference signal and stabilize improvement, ECO optionally constructs winner-loser pairs by applying local search (2-opt/3-opt) to a sampled solution and preferring the refined tour. Architecturally, ECO replaces the typical Transformer backbone with a “mixed Mamba” encoder-decoder: an S6 (input-dependent) Mamba encoder run in recurrent/scan mode and an S4 (time-invariant) Mamba decoder run in convolution/parallel mode, aiming for linear memory scaling and higher throughput. Experiments on synthetic TSP (N up to 5000) and CVRP (N up to 1000) compare solution quality, inference time, convergence speed, and memory/throughput scaling against several learning baselines and classical solvers; ablations isolate SFT, DPO, and local-search bootstrapping contributions.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The method is conceptually coherent: SFT addresses cold-start for preference learning; DPO provides a stable, critic-free optimization objective; local-search–augmented pairs provide a clean margin; and Mamba is leveraged for claimed linear memory scaling. The paper includes an explicit DPO objective, pseudocode, and an appendix deriving the DPO form and giving gradient intuition.
- Weaknesses: Several key experimental and methodological details are under-specified or potentially inconsistent, limiting the ability to verify correctness.
  1) “Offline” vs “self-play rollout” ambiguity: Phase II is described as offline, but the algorithm generates K samples from the *current* policy every iteration (Alg. 1 line 18), i.e., an on-policy data generation loop. It may still be “offline” in the sense of using a preference buffer and not interleaving environment steps, but in NCO the environment is the problem instance itself; the distinction from standard online RL is not crisply formalized.
  2) Architecture-description mismatch for decoding: The decoder description says it uses offline routed maps to reorder embeddings (Sec. 3.3.2) and then produces logits masked to prevent revisits. It is unclear how this supports *inference*, where no routed map exists a priori. If the decoder requires a full route permutation as input, that seems incompatible with autoregressive construction at test time. If instead the “routed map” is only for teacher-forcing during training and inference uses incremental ordering, the paper should explicitly define the inference procedure.
  3) Preference data construction details: For the non-LS branch, the winner is argmin and loser is argmax among K samples. This creates an extremely wide pair but may bias learning toward distribution tails; there is no analysis of sensitivity to K or alternative pairing schemes.
  4) Fairness/controls: The “control variate baseline” for memory/throughput replaces Mamba with a Transformer while keeping pipelines identical, but the exact Transformer configuration (layers/width, attention type, use of flash-attention, KV cache, etc.) is not specified. This matters because efficiency claims hinge on implementation choices.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well structured (problem, method, experiments, ablations), with clear equations for SFT and DPO and a helpful algorithm box. Figures and tables directly support the efficiency narrative.
- Weaknesses: Some core explanations are confusing and occasionally contradictory.
  - The decoder’s dependence on “offline routed map” is the most significant clarity issue.
  - “Offline” is used in multiple senses (offline dataset for SFT; iterative self-generated data for DPO; offline vs online RL), but the operational definition is not stated precisely.
  - Some hyperparameter details conflict: main text says LS mixing ratio α=0.3, while Appendix B.3 says augmented pairs constitute 20% of data.

Significance:
- Strengths: The paper targets an important and practical bottleneck for NCO—memory scaling and throughput at large N—supported by stress tests up to N=10,000. If the architecture/training indeed yields similar quality with much better resource usage, this is meaningful for large-scale routing.
- Weaknesses: Quality results are mixed. ECO without applying local search at inference is notably worse than the strongest learning baseline (e.g., GFlowNet-HBG) on several settings in Table 1, and ECO’s best numbers often rely on adding local search at inference, which changes the compute profile and complicates claims of “internalizing” local search. The paper also does not evaluate generalization beyond the training distribution or other CO tasks.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of (i) DPO-style preference optimization with (ii) Mamba-based encoder-decoder for NCO and (iii) local-search–amplified preference pairs is a novel integration within the scope of this paper. The mixed S6/S4 encoder/decoder design is also a specific architectural choice tailored to training/inference efficiency.
- Weaknesses: Parts are incremental in isolation (SFT warm-start; local search bootstrapping; iterative reference updates), and the paper acknowledges concurrent DPO-for-NCO works. The novelty thus rests mainly on the efficiency-motivated system design and empirical profiling.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Inference procedure: How does ECO decode a route at test time without an “offline routed map” to permute H into H′ (Sec. 3.3.2)? Please provide the step-by-step inference algorithm and clarify what is fed to the S4 decoder at each step.
2) What exactly is “offline” about Phase II? Alg. 1 samples K solutions from the current policy each iteration (self-play). Is the main efficiency gain from removing the critic and enabling larger batches, from decoupling rollout/training, or from something else? A precise definition and timing breakdown (data gen vs optimization) would help.
3) Efficiency comparison details: What is the exact Transformer baseline used in Fig. 3 (layers, hidden size, attention implementation)? Was flash-attention/KV-cache used? Without this, it is hard to interpret the magnitude of throughput gains.
4) Local search usage and claims of “internalization”: Do you have evidence that the model alone (without LS at inference) learns the same structural improvements? For example, compare ECO vs ECO(Local search) on edge-crossing metrics or on performance as LS budget varies.
5) Clarify the LS mixing ratio discrepancy: main text states α=0.3 while Appendix B.3 says 20% augmented pairs. Which is correct in the reported experiments (Table 1/Table 2)?
review.limitations: No. The impact/limitations statement is effectively empty (“none… must be specifically highlighted”). At minimum, the authors should discuss: (i) environmental/compute cost tradeoffs (offline generation with K samples plus LS can be expensive), (ii) reliance on strong solvers (LKH-3) for SFT labels and how that affects applicability to problems without good heuristics, (iii) potential distribution shift/generalization limits (trained on synthetic instances), and (iv) any misuse risks (e.g., logistics/routing optimization in sensitive contexts).

title: Stochastic Interpolants in Hilbert Spaces

review.summary: The paper generalizes stochastic interpolants (SIs)—processes of the form x_t = α(t)x_0 + β(t)x_1 + γ(t)z—to infinite-dimensional, separable Hilbert spaces. It identifies measure-theoretic obstacles (trace-class noise, lack of Lebesgue measure, mutual singularity of time-marginals) and proposes an infinite-dimensional formulation based on trace-class Gaussian noise and conditional expectations rather than scores. A central contribution is a Conditional Bridge SDE (CB-SDE) whose drift is expressed via a “velocity” term and a “denoiser” term defined as conditional expectations given (x_0, x_t), and which is intended to transport an initial function x_0 to the correct conditional target law of x_1 given x_0. The paper provides sufficient conditions for well-posedness (existence and, under additional assumptions, strong uniqueness) and derives a Wasserstein-2 error bound relating distributional error of generated samples to regression error in learned velocity/denoiser fields. Practically, it introduces a time-change construction to regularize endpoint singularities in the drift/coefficients. Empirically, it evaluates on 1D and 2D PDE forward/inverse problems using neural operators, comparing to finite-dimensional SIs and diffusion-model baselines, and reports competitive to state-of-the-art results (notably on Navier–Stokes) and an ablation showing time-change is critical for stability.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness (good): The paper carefully formulates SIs in Hilbert spaces with trace-class Gaussian noise and explicitly discusses key infinite-dimensional pathologies (no Lebesgue density; Feldman–Hajek singularity under rescaling). The CB-SDE drift is defined through conditional expectations (velocity/denoiser), and Theorem 2 establishes marginal correctness of the conditional bridge given existence/uniqueness in law and uniqueness of the associated infinite-dimensional Fokker–Planck equation. The well-posedness analysis is nontrivial: Proposition 4 provides HC-Lipschitz conditions under either (i) a strong density/strong convexity assumption (Hypothesis 3) or (ii) bounded support in Cameron–Martin norm; Theorem 5 gives existence on compact subintervals; Theorem 6 gives a sufficient uniqueness condition via independence along an eigenbasis. The Wasserstein bound (Theorem 8) is a useful quantitative guarantee, and the time-change (Lemma 7) addresses coefficient blow-ups.

However, several technical requirements are strong and sometimes partially assumed rather than proved within the framework’s most general setting: (a) Theorem 2 assumes uniqueness solvability of the infinite-dimensional Fokker–Planck equation, and this is pivotal for correctness; (b) strong uniqueness (Theorem 6) requires a factorization/independence assumption along the eigenbasis of C, which may not match the coupled PDE datasets used; (c) for the W2 bound, assumption (ii) requires H-norm Lipschitzness of learned models, while the well-posedness theory is built around HC-Lipschitzness—this mismatch is not fully reconciled, and it is not shown that the true drift is Lipschitz in H-norm (only in HC-norm). The time-change is justified for controlling coefficients, but the practical choice/verification of its conditions for arbitrary γ is not fully operationalized beyond the specific γ(t)=sqrt(bt(1-t)) case.

Presentation (good): The narrative is well structured: challenges → definitions → conditional bridge → well-posedness → learning → time change → bounds → experiments. Key definitions are explicit and the appendix contains detailed proofs and implementation details. Still, some notation is occasionally inconsistent/overloaded (e.g., switching between x_t and X_t; occasional typos like using “φ˜”/“φe” inconsistently in the theorem statement/proof; and the W2 theorem’s constants C(t) differ slightly between main text and appendix). The experimental section is clear but limited in scope (two main 2D benchmarks and one 1D ablation).

Significance (good): A rigorous SI framework in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, especially with conditional bridges for coupled data, is potentially impactful for function-valued generative modeling and scientific ML. The time-change device and the W2 regression-to-distribution bound are practically relevant. Nonetheless, the practical significance is somewhat tempered by the strength of assumptions needed for theory (data in HC, strong convexity/density, eigenbasis independence) and by the modest breadth of empirical validation (PDE benchmarks only).

Originality (good): The paper’s combination of (i) SI formulation that avoids score densities via conditional expectations, (ii) explicit conditional bridge construction for coupled source/target distributions in Hilbert space, (iii) well-posedness conditions in the Cameron–Martin geometry, and (iv) time-change regularization plus W2 error bounds appears novel within the SI context as presented. The conditional-bridge focus (as distinct from marginal bridges) is a meaningful extension over finite-dimensional SI treatments discussed by the authors.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Theorem 6 (strong uniqueness) assumes µ1 factorizes along the eigenbasis of C (mutual independence of coefficients). Do your PDE datasets (Darcy binary permeability; Navier–Stokes vorticity fields) satisfy this even approximately? If not, what theoretical guarantee (weak uniqueness, uniqueness in law, or empirical evidence) supports using a single well-defined CB-SDE at inference?

2) Theorem 2 relies on uniqueness solvability of the associated infinite-dimensional Fokker–Planck equation, which is assumed. Can you specify verifiable sufficient conditions (in your setting/drift form) under which this uniqueness holds, and do your Proposition 4 conditions imply them?

3) There is a norm mismatch: well-posedness is developed via HC-Lipschitz drift, while Theorem 8 assumes the learned approximations are Lipschitz in the H-norm and uses H-norm errors A(s),B(s). Can you clarify why H-norm Lipschitzness is the right condition for the bound, and whether HC-Lipschitzness (or mixed norms) would be more natural/needed in infinite dimensions?

4) Conditional bridge training: the CB drift uses conditioning on (x0, x_t), but the proposed losses (18)-(19) regress functions of (x_t,t) only (as in standard SI) rather than (x0,x_t,t). Is this a typo/oversight in the learning section, or are you actually learning the marginal bridge in experiments? If you do learn conditional fields, please detail the exact inputs to φθ and ηϕ used in all experiments.

5) In experiments, how is the covariance operator C (via GP kernel lengthscale ℓ) chosen/tuned, and how sensitive are results to ℓ? The paper suggests a “sweet spot” but provides limited quantitative sensitivity analysis on the main 2D tasks.
review.limitations: No. The limitations discussion is brief and the Impact Statement asserts no specific societal consequences. The paper should more explicitly discuss (i) the restrictiveness/practical validity of assumptions (x1 in HC; strong convexity/density; eigenbasis independence) and what failure modes occur when they are violated; (ii) compute and scalability costs (two networks, many function evaluations; comparison to baselines with much larger NFE); (iii) domain limitations (fixed uniform grids; sensor placement assumptions); and (iv) potential downstream risks of functional generative models in scientific settings (e.g., overconfident surrogate solutions, misuse in decision-making) and recommended safeguards (uncertainty reporting, calibration, validation against solvers).

title: Chunk-Guided Q-Learning

review.summary: The paper proposes Chunk-Guided Q-Learning (CGQ) for offline RL in long-horizon tasks. CGQ trains (i) an auxiliary action-chunked critic using h-step chunked TD backups and an action-chunked policy (via QC-FQL), and (ii) the main single-step critic with the standard 1-step TD loss plus a regularization term that distills from the chunked critic using an upper-expectile (asymmetric) regression. The intent is to leverage chunked backups for more stable long-range propagation while retaining a single-step critic/policy class that can represent reactive behavior and stitch trajectories. The paper provides an analysis of a regularized stochastic Bellman-iteration process, deriving an error bound that interpolates between noise-driven error accumulation and bias from regularizing toward a potentially suboptimal chunked critic, and argues there exists a finite regularization weight that can improve over both extremes under a curvature condition. Empirically, CGQ is evaluated on OGBench manipulation and navigation tasks, showing strong gains on manipulation (especially longer-horizon cube tasks) and weaker/negative results on navigation/locomotion; the paper also includes ablations on chunk size, regularization weight, and alternative blending designs.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Clear and simple algorithmic idea: use a chunked critic as an auxiliary “stabilizer” while keeping the deployed critic/policy single-step. The method is easy to implement on top of existing actor-critic offline RL pipelines.
- Motivating trade-off is well articulated and supported by a didactic gridworld example illustrating (a) compounding bootstrapping error in 1-step TD and (b) structural suboptimality of open-loop chunk evaluation.
- Empirical evaluation on OGBench manipulation shows large improvements over both a strong single-step baseline (FQL/NFQL) and chunked baselines (QC-FQL/DEAS/DQC) on several long-horizon categories (cube-triple/quadruple).
- Useful ablations: varying chunk size h, regularization strength β, expectile τ, and comparisons to alternative integration designs (distill-only, max, opposite).

Weaknesses (by dimension):

Soundness (fair):
- The theoretical analysis models learning as a stochastic iterative application of an abstract contraction operator plus additive noise, and then introduces a linear convex-combination regularization toward a fixed Qc. This provides intuition, but it is not tightly matched to the practical algorithm: in CGQ, Qc is learned concurrently (and depends on data, function approximation, and policy learning), and the regularizer uses an expectile loss (asymmetric) rather than the simple convex combination analyzed. Consequently, the bound is more of a qualitative justification than a formal guarantee for the proposed procedure.
- The method depends critically on the quality of the chunked critic; the paper documents negative results on navigation and attributes them to difficulty in chunked policy learning corrupting the chunked critic, but there is no principled mechanism to detect/mitigate harmful guidance beyond tuning β.

Presentation (good):
- Overall the paper is readable, with a clear problem statement, method section, and experimental details/hyperparameters. Figures and the “Q&A” format help clarify design choices.
- Some notational/definition mismatches make the implementation slightly harder to audit: e.g., in preliminaries Eq. (2) uses sampling (st, at, st+h)∼D but later switches to Dh; the relationship between the dataset transitions and chunk sampling is not fully formalized.

Significance (good):
- If the reported gains on OGBench manipulation generalize, the approach is a practical improvement for long-horizon offline RL where bootstrapping error is severe. The idea of using chunked backups only as an auxiliary signal (rather than committing to a chunked policy) is potentially impactful for robotic manipulation.
- However, the failure on navigation tasks suggests the method’s benefits may be domain-dependent; without a more robust mechanism for when/how to trust chunk guidance, the impact could be limited to settings where chunked critics are reliably trainable.

Originality (good):
- The core idea—regularizing a single-step critic toward a separately trained chunk-based critic—is a novel and clean way to combine horizon reduction benefits with reactive policy expressivity. While it is conceptually related to multi-step/TD(λ)-style blending and to distillation approaches (e.g., chunk critic distillation), the specific “chunk-guided single-step TD + expectile distillation” design and analysis focus appear to be a distinct contribution in the paper’s framing and experiments.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Regularizer mismatch to theory: The analysis treats the update as an explicit convex combination toward a fixed Qc, but the implemented method uses expectile regression toward a concurrently learned Qϕc. Can you clarify the precise objective minimized by the critic in practice (e.g., is it exactly Eq. (12) with expectile loss), and provide evidence that the analyzed phenomenon tracks the real training dynamics (e.g., by plotting measures of ∥Qϕ−Qϕc∥ and critic error proxies versus β)?

2) Chunked critic reliability: Since navigation failures are attributed to an unreliable chunked critic (due to difficulty of learning chunked policies), do you have diagnostics showing Qϕc is poor (e.g., Bellman error, disagreement between ensemble members, or downstream value calibration)? Could you quantify when guidance becomes harmful and whether a simple gating (e.g., based on critic uncertainty/disagreement) fixes the negative results?

3) Fairness of baseline comparisons in Table 1: Many baseline numbers are copied from prior work (without ±) and may use different compute, architectures, or tuning protocols. Can you confirm which baselines were re-run under the same codebase/training budget as CGQ for each task category, and provide a version of the main table restricted to methods evaluated under the same protocol (or at least matched architectures/budgets)?

4) Sensitivity/generalization of β and h: β is shown crucial (Fig. 5) and per-task tuned (Table 9). How well does a single β (and h) transfer across tasks within a category (e.g., across the 5 cube-double tasks) or across manipulation categories? Would performance remain competitive under a fixed global β/h choice?

5) Policy extraction coupling: CGQ trains πωc (chunked) and πω (single-step) concurrently. How sensitive are results to the strength of the chunked policy constraint α and to potential instability from training two flow models? Have you tried training Qϕc with a fixed behavior-chunk policy (no policy improvement) to isolate whether chunked policy learning is necessary for useful guidance?
review.limitations: Partially. The paper includes a short limitations paragraph (chunked critic inaccuracies can hurt; β tuning difficulty) and an impact statement that claims no immediate negative societal impacts. However, the limitations discussion could be strengthened by (i) more explicit guidance on when CGQ is expected to fail (e.g., domains requiring highly reactive control / where chunked policy learning is unreliable), (ii) an analysis of hyperparameter transfer and compute overhead from training auxiliary chunked components, and (iii) a more concrete discussion of risks in safety-critical deployment (e.g., offline learned policies with misestimated values) and how the method might exacerbate or mitigate them.

title: How Attention Sinks Emerge in Large Language Models: An Interpretability Perspective

review.summary: The paper investigates the “position-zero” (P0) attention sink in autoregressive transformer LLMs, i.e., the consistent over-attention to the first token in the sequence. It argues that while a [BOS] token can induce a shallow-layer sink, modern LLMs exhibit a robust P0 sink even without [BOS], implying the sink is driven by structural properties rather than token semantics. The authors propose and analyze a mechanistic explanation termed the P0-Sink Circuit: within two transformer blocks, the model (i) identifies position 0 using causal-mask asymmetry via broadly-averaging attention behavior and (ii) amplifies the position-0 residual-stream representation into a high-norm, near-fixed-direction vector via MLPs, which then attracts attention in later layers. The paper supports these claims with ablations removing [BOS] in multiple pretrained models, representation analyses (norm growth, cosine similarity, PCA/t-SNE clustering), a simplified theoretical model linking attention-output norms to sequence length under a cone model of value vectors, and training-trace analysis of a 30B-A3B MoE model trained from scratch showing a three-stage emergence (middle-layer emergence, shallow diffusion, then concentration into first two layers).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The central empirical observation (P0 sink persists without [BOS] and re-emerges after a couple layers) is demonstrated across several model families with consistent diagnostics: attention heatmaps, layerwise hidden-state ℓ2 norms, and directional consistency measures. The proposed two-block “circuit” is plausibly supported by (a) early separation/clustering of position-0 hidden states prior to strong MLP amplification, and (b) subsequent strong norm amplification and direction stabilization at P0. The analysis connecting large norm + pre-norm RMSNorm to directional stability via the Jacobian (Eq. 1–5) is clear and mathematically reasonable.
- Weaknesses: The paper’s “circuit” is mostly descriptive/phenomenological rather than a rigorously verified causal mechanism. There is limited direct intervention evidence that the specific identified components are necessary/sufficient (e.g., targeted edits to the attention/MLP parameters that disrupt identification vs amplification while keeping other behaviors intact). Head ablations shown suggest no single local head is responsible, but do not isolate the putative “uniform averaging heads” as a causal driver. The cone model and Eq. 11 primarily explain a trend in attention-output norm vs sequence length, but the link from that trend to “position-zero identification” is indirect, and assumptions (independence, cone geometry, sparsity behavior of p) are not validated quantitatively in the paper.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The narrative is coherent: (1) establish sink without [BOS], (2) characterize fixed-direction/high-norm P0 representation, (3) propose identification via causal asymmetry, (4) show training dynamics. Figures are plentiful and generally align with claims.
- Weaknesses: Key experimental details are underspecified for reproducibility: the exact procedure for “[BOS] removal” in pretrained models (re-tokenization? dropping token id? shifting positions?) and evaluation protocol for Table 1 are not fully formalized; the “Sink Circuit” definition could be sharper (what measurable criteria define successful identification and amplification?). The dataset setup is unusual (first 1024 samples from the first parquet file, max length 64), raising questions about representativeness; this choice is stated but not justified.

Significance:
- Strengths: Understanding attention sinks is relevant both for interpretability and for practical long-context methods that exploit sinks. The training-trace analysis suggesting sink-stage as a convergence indicator is potentially useful.
- Weaknesses: The paper does not convincingly demonstrate that the proposed diagnostics improve model development or downstream performance; the “convergence indicator” claim remains speculative with limited validation (Appendix C is referenced but not concretely tied to quantitative convergence/performance metrics in the main text).

Originality:
- Strengths: The explicit framing of a two-block positional identification + norm amplification circuit (P0-Sink Circuit) and the training-stage characterization in a large-from-scratch MoE trace go beyond prior observational accounts in the related-work section.
- Weaknesses: Several ingredients (norm amplification at BOS/P0, sinks helping long-context streaming, association with pre-norm stability) are closely related to prior hypotheses; the novelty lies more in consolidating them into a circuit narrative plus training-trace staging than in introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

Overall, the work is a strong empirical interpretability study with an appealing mechanistic story, but it would benefit from more definitive causal interventions and clearer, more reproducible operationalization of the “circuit.”
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How exactly is “[BOS] removal” implemented for models trained with a BOS token (both for attention/norm analyses and for the loss experiments in Table 1)? Please specify tokenization, positional indexing, and whether the model is run with shifted positions or with a “missing” embedding at position 0.
2) What are the minimal causal interventions supporting necessity/sufficiency of the two claimed stages (position-0 identification in attention; amplification/fixing direction in MLP)? For example, can you selectively suppress the layer-1 (or layer-0/1) MLP up-projection directions responsible for the fixed P0 vector and show the sink disappears while other behaviors remain?
3) The identification mechanism attributes the effect to “uniform averaging” attention heads under causal masking. Can you define a quantitative criterion for “uniform averaging heads” and report ablations/interventions on that subset (rather than individual local heads) to test whether they are necessary for early P0 clustering?
4) For the 30B-A3B training traces, how consistent is the three-stage process across random seeds, data orderings, or modest hyperparameter changes? If it is not consistent, what conditions govern whether/when the circuit concentrates into the first two layers?
5) The paper suggests sink-stage could be used as a pretraining convergence indicator. Do you have quantitative evidence correlating the identified sink-stage transitions with standard convergence/progress metrics (e.g., validation loss slope, downstream evals, or in-training compute-optimality proxies) beyond the qualitative Appendix C discussion?
review.limitations: No. The paper includes an “Impact Statement” header but does not provide a substantive limitations / societal impact discussion in the provided text. At minimum, it should: (i) discuss how attention-sink manipulation or diagnostic use might fail across architectures (e.g., sliding-window/hybrid attention) and across context lengths beyond 64; (ii) clarify that findings are based on a small, non-random dataset slice and may not generalize; (iii) discuss potential misuse (e.g., using sink-based diagnostics to justify premature stopping or to make claims about model quality without task evaluations), and potential impacts on downstream applications that rely on special treatment of initial tokens.

title: Do Diffusion Models Dream of Electric Planes? Discrete and Continuous Simulation-Based Inference for Aircraft Design

review.summary:
The paper tackles simulation-based inference (SBI) for conceptual eVTOL aircraft design where the latent design includes (i) discrete topological choices (144 configurations) and (ii) a topology-dependent set of continuous parameters (up to ~126–136 dimensions), with simulator outputs consisting of 10 summary performance statistics from SUAVE. The authors propose a hierarchical posterior factorization p(\theta,\tau\mid x)=p(\theta\mid \tau,x)p(\tau\mid x) and instantiate it with two diffusion-transformer models.

First, MixeDiT models the joint of topology and observations and is used to sample from p(\tau\mid x). It combines (a) an RDLM-style discrete diffusion head operating via a continuous manifold representation of categorical distributions, and (b) a continuous diffusion head for the observations, trained with a weighted combination of discrete cross-entropy and continuous denoising loss.

Second, MaskeDiT extends the Simformer “all-in-one” diffusion-SBI approach to variable-dimensional parameter spaces by introducing a topology mask that suppresses tokens/attention edges for absent components, enabling a single model to learn across many topologies. The paper also contributes a dataset generation pipeline (tree/JSON aircraft grammar + feasibility filters + SUAVE evaluation) resulting in 30,276 valid designs from 300k proposals, and provides quantitative and qualitative evaluations including posterior predictive checks and several design-trend case studies.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The hierarchical decomposition is natural for variable-dimensional parameters and is clearly tied to the modeling choices (MixeDiT for p(\tau\mid x), MaskeDiT for p(\theta\mid\tau,x)). The masking mechanism in MaskeDiT is a reasonable adaptation of transformer-based diffusion SBI to handle missing components, with masking applied consistently in attention and in the loss. The evaluation includes both distributional tests (MMD, C2ST) and posterior predictive checks by re-simulating generated designs in SUAVE.
- Weaknesses: Several methodological details that affect correctness are underspecified or potentially inconsistent. For example, the notation around diffusion endpoints/timesteps for MixeDiT and MaskeDiT is easy to confuse (e.g., t=0 as noise vs t=1 as data, and separate t_\tau and t_x in MixeDiT), and the description of how p(\tau\mid x) is obtained via a model trained on p(\tau,x) is not fully explicit about conditioning implementation beyond “fix x and set t_x=1”. The training objective for MixeDiT combines discrete and continuous processes but does not discuss whether/why independent time sampling and a single shared transformer input are sufficient to learn the correct conditional over topologies for arbitrary x. The paper also includes a “clamp out-of-distribution values” post-processing step in the sampling procedure; it is unclear how often this happens and whether it materially affects PPC results.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The overall pipeline and the motivation (mixed discrete/continuous + variable dimensional SBI) are well communicated, with a clear architecture diagram and explicit algorithms in the appendix. The dataset generation details, including feasibility checks and sources of stochasticity, are unusually thorough for an ML-for-science/design paper.
- Weaknesses: There are occasional inconsistencies and small errors that reduce clarity (e.g., D_\tau is stated as max 126 in one place and d_max=136 elsewhere; some algorithm steps appear to have typos in mask definitions; Table 1 vs Table 3 numbering mismatch in the main text). The evaluation section could be structured more cleanly to separate (i) topology modeling, (ii) per-topology continuous posterior modeling, and (iii) end-to-end conditional generation.

Significance:
- Strengths: The work addresses a real, multi-physics design setting with mixed discrete/continuous structure and high-dimensional parameters, and proposes a practical method to amortize expensive simulation. The end-to-end posterior predictive checking using an established conceptual design simulator (SUAVE) and the speed comparison are compelling for the “SBI for engineering design” community.
- Weaknesses: The demonstrated speedup comparison uses CPU-only SUAVE vs GPU sampling, which is pragmatic but makes it hard to attribute gains purely to amortization (vs hardware). Also, the reported “≥10×” speedup for 100 samples is based on a single SUAVE case run 100 times, which may not reflect real throughput when designs vary and may influence convergence/runtime.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of (1) RDLM-style discrete diffusion in continuous manifold space for topology sampling and (2) a topology-conditioned masking scheme enabling a single diffusion-SBI model across variable-dimensional parameterizations is a novel system-level contribution in the context of SBI for design. The end-to-end hierarchical diffusion SBI for an aerospace conceptual design pipeline (including topology changes) appears to be beyond the typical fixed-structure SBI benchmarks.
- Weaknesses: MaskeDiT is conceptually an extension of Simformer via additional masking; while useful, the novelty hinges on the specific variable-topology setting and empirical demonstration rather than fundamentally new diffusion theory.

Overall, the paper is technically interesting and well-motivated, with strong empirical ambition and a valuable dataset/pipeline. The main limitations are around clarity/rigor of the probabilistic conditioning story for MixeDiT, and some evaluation gaps that make it hard to judge whether the learned distributions are well calibrated beyond matching certain summary statistics and qualitative trends.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How often does the “clamp out-of-distribution values to nearest valid value” step (Alg. 5, step 3) activate during sampling, and how much do posterior predictive checks change if you disallow clamping (e.g., reject and resample instead)?

2) For MixeDiT, can you precisely describe how conditioning on a target x* is implemented during sampling (beyond “set t_x=1 and fix x”)? In particular, is x held fixed throughout the reverse-time integration while \tau diffuses, and does the sampler still update an x-state internally?

3) The paper reports D_\tau max values inconsistently (126 vs 136). What is the exact tokenization dimension used by MaskeDiT (d_max), how many of those tokens correspond to \theta vs x, and how are “unused” tokens distributed across topologies?

4) In the MaskeDiT vs NLE comparison, NLE is trained per-topology with default hyperparameters. Did you tune NLE at all, and do the conclusions hold when allowing NLE comparable compute/model selection? Also, why is the joint C2ST substantially above 0.5 (≈0.74–0.78) for both methods—does this indicate noticeable mismatch?

5) For end-to-end p(\theta,\tau\mid x) sampling, do you have any quantitative evaluation of p(\tau\mid x) beyond the two mass-conditioning examples (e.g., across many x conditions and multiple topology features), and can you report accuracy/calibration of topology posterior trends under different x constraints?
review.limitations:
Partially yes: the paper includes an impact statement and explicitly discusses limitations of the dataset/simulator fidelity (e.g., SUAVE’s low-fidelity models and potential large errors for unconventional configurations) and acknowledges that many generated designs may be unreasonable in reality.

Suggestions: (i) Discuss more explicitly how the model might amplify biases introduced by the hand-specified generative prior and rejection filters (e.g., topology frequency distortions) and how this affects posterior interpretation. (ii) Clarify potential misuse concerns: even conceptual aircraft generation can be dual-use; propose concrete safeguards (e.g., restricting mission profiles or performance objectives, or watermarking generated concepts). (iii) Add limitations about evaluation: PPC uses the same simulator family used to label the dataset, so it does not validate real-world correctness; consider stating this more directly.

title: Word Recovery in Large Language Models Enables Character-Level Tokenization Robustness

review.summary: The paper investigates why LLMs trained with standard subword tokenization can still perform reasonably well when inputs are provided at the character level. The authors propose that models internally reconstruct (“recover”) canonical word/subword token identities from character sequences. They (i) define a layerwise word recovery score using LogitLens-style decoding of hidden states into vocabulary tokens and measuring which canonical tokens become decodable, (ii) test causal importance by removing the residual-stream component aligned with the output-embedding direction of a recovered token over the character span corresponding to that token, and measuring downstream QA accuracy drops as a function of intervention layer, and (iii) analyze attention by masking “in-group” attention (attention among characters belonging to the same canonical token span) and showing that early-layer masking reduces both recovery scores and task accuracy. Experiments cover three instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2-9B-It, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) and four multiple-choice QA datasets (ARC-E, ARC-C, CSQA, OpenbookQA).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The work goes beyond behavioral robustness and attempts a mechanistic account with (a) a measurable proxy for “recovery,” (b) causal interventions in representation space, and (c) a second causal test via attention masking. The layer-sweep intervention design (starting at layer ℓ0 through end) is a reasonable way to localize when information becomes necessary. The appendix addresses two key measurement concerns: sensitivity to top-K and potential overcounting from global decoding by providing an in-group decoding variant.
- Weaknesses / concerns: (1) The causal subspace removal assumes that the output embedding vector w_t is a meaningful and sufficiently specific “token identity” direction; however, no normalization details are provided (e.g., whether w_t is unit-norm) and the update h ← h − <h,w_t> w_t is only a true orthogonal projection if w_t is normalized. If not, the magnitude of removal is scale-dependent and may confound interpretation. (2) It is unclear how target tokens t are selected for intervention during evaluation (all tokens? a subset? which ones when duplicates removed?); the paper describes the mechanism but not the exact protocol used to produce Figures 3–5, which matters for reproducibility and for interpreting effect sizes. (3) The “recovery score” is set-based over unique canonical tokens, discarding positional alignment and frequency; this may inflate perceived recovery and makes it harder to connect recovery to specific computation (though Appendix B partially addresses spurious-position concerns).

Presentation:
- Strengths: The narrative is clear: define recovery → measure it → test causality via representation removal → test mechanism via attention masking. Figures (recovery curves; accuracy under interventions) directly support the claims. The appendix anticipates likely critiques about K and span-localization.
- Weaknesses: Some experimental and implementation details are underspecified: exact character-level tokenization procedure (e.g., inclusion of spaces, punctuation handling), prompts/format for multiple-choice QA, decoding/generation settings during evaluation, and details of the intervention (which tokens intervened on, how many per example, whether applied to all heads/layers exactly as described). These omissions limit reproducibility.

Significance:
- Strengths: If correct, the work provides a concrete mechanistic explanation for an increasingly important phenomenon (robustness to tokenization changes), and connects it to actionable architectural behavior (early in-group attention). This can influence how the community thinks about tokenizer “limitations” and how interpretability tools can analyze tokenization effects.
- Weaknesses: The demonstrated scope is limited to English multiple-choice QA benchmarks and three instruction-tuned models. It’s unclear whether the mechanism generalizes to other tasks (generation, long-context, code), languages, or more adversarial character-level perturbations.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of (i) a specific operationalization of “word recovery,” (ii) causal tests tied to recovered token directions, and (iii) targeted in-group attention masking framed explicitly around canonical-token spans is a fairly novel package aimed at explaining tokenization robustness mechanistically.
- Weaknesses: The decoding approach is closely related to existing LogitLens ideas; novelty comes primarily from the framing (tokenization robustness) and the particular interventions rather than an entirely new interpretability methodology.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) In the residual-stream removal intervention, is w_t normalized (or do you use a true projection h − (<h,w_t>/<w_t,w_t>) w_t)? If not, how sensitive are the results to token-embedding norms, and could effects be driven by removing a large-norm direction rather than “token identity” per se?
2) What is the exact intervention protocol used to generate Figures 3–5: which canonical tokens t are intervened on per example (all tokens in T, only recovered ones, a fixed subset such as question tokens, or something else)? How do you aggregate across tokens/spans to produce a single accuracy curve?
3) How exactly is character-level tokenization implemented (e.g., are spaces separate tokens, do you preserve “_” markers used by some tokenizers, how are multi-byte/Unicode characters handled)? Since in-group spans depend on canonical token boundaries, please clarify the mapping from canonical tokens to character spans.
4) For in-group attention masking, is masking applied to all heads at the masked layers? Do you renormalize attention in a particular way after setting in-group logits to −∞, and does the effect persist if you mask only a subset of heads?
5) Do the main conclusions still hold when recovery is defined positionally (e.g., requiring token t to be decoded primarily within its own span and near-correct relative position) rather than set-based over unique tokens? Appendix B addresses span restriction, but not positional alignment beyond span membership.
review.limitations: Partially. The paper includes a brief impact statement but does not meaningfully discuss limitations beyond a small decoding ablation. I suggest adding: (i) clearer scope limits (English QA only; three instruction-tuned models; character-level tokenization as a specific non-canonical setting), (ii) discussion of alternative explanations/confounds for the causal interventions (e.g., embedding-direction removal as a broad semantic perturbation; norm effects), (iii) analysis of generalization to other tasks/languages or longer contexts, and (iv) potential misuse considerations (e.g., mechanistic insights potentially aiding adversarial manipulation or evasion, even if indirect).

title: Elucidating the Design Space of Flow Matching for Cellular Microscopy

review.summary:
This paper studies flow-matching/diffusion-style generative models for high-content cellular microscopy under biological perturbations, with an emphasis on identifying robust design choices for (i) generation conditioned on seen perturbations and (ii) virtual screening for unseen perturbations.

The authors first propose a conceptual decomposition for unseen-perturbation generation into a “base generative model error” term (quality/coverage for seen perturbations) and a “perturbation representation/encoder error” term (how well a perturbation embedding maps into the model’s conditioning space). They then conduct an extensive empirical sweep on RxRx1 to simplify and improve training recipes: switching from control-to-perturbed flows to standard noise-to-data flows, using explicit experiment-label conditioning to capture batch effects, analyzing counterfactual-style sampling, testing minibatch OT couplings and alternative interpolants, and introducing a stabilized pixel-space diffusion transformer variant (“MiT”) plus large-scale pretraining on Phenoprints.

Finally, for BBBC021 the paper evaluates conditioning strategies for unseen small molecules by freezing the base model and learning an adaptor from molecular features (Morgan fingerprints or MolGPS embeddings) into the model’s conditioning space, reporting improved FID/KID on the standard seen/unseen splits and arguing that molecular representations are a key bottleneck for virtual screening.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The empirical methodology is generally careful and reproducible within the paper’s scope. The authors validate their FID/KID pipelines by reproducing prior reported numbers, clearly define the RxRx1/BBBC021 splits used (matching prior work), and provide detailed training/inference hyperparameters, compute estimates, and guidance/solver settings. The RxRx1 ablation grid is fairly comprehensive across conditioning, flow construction, OT couplings, interpolants, architecture stability interventions, and pretraining.
- Weaknesses: The theoretical result in §3 is essentially a Lipschitz + triangle-inequality bound, and Assumption 1 (“coverage”) hides the core difficulty; it is more a framing device than an analysis that yields testable predictions. More importantly, the “unseen molecules” setup in §5 is only loosely tied to the bound: the paper does not quantify or estimate either term (ϵ_base, ϵ_G) nor validate the Lipschitz-style dependence empirically (e.g., by measuring output distribution shift as adaptor error varies). On the experimental side, the use of only FID/KID-style metrics (plus DinoV2 variants for RxRx1) leaves open whether improvements correspond to better perturbation-specific biological signal rather than improved marginal realism; the qualitative discussion for a single unseen compound is suggestive but not systematically evaluated.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is well-structured (theory framing → RxRx1 recipe → BBBC021 generalization), and the ablations are presented clearly in tables with compute and configuration labels. The appendices provide unusually concrete details (projection from 6-channel to RGB for evaluation, solver choices, guidance sweeps, stability ablations).
- Weaknesses: Some claims are stronger than what is directly supported. For example, “many popular techniques are unnecessary and can even hurt performance” is supported for the particular benchmarks/settings tested, but the conclusions are occasionally phrased more generally than the experiments justify. Also, the BBBC021 adaptor training description implies the base model is partially unfrozen (“except AdaLN modulation layers”) but the exact set of trainable parameters and its effect on fairness vs prior methods (which may train end-to-end) could be stated more explicitly.

Significance:
- Strengths: The work provides a pragmatic, simplified recipe for training high-fidelity conditional microscopy generators and demonstrates large gains on established benchmarks, including scaling to substantially higher compute and data via Phenoprints pretraining. The finding that simple N→D training with explicit experiment conditioning can outperform C→P constructions (and that OT couplings/interpolant variants don’t help here) is a useful message for practitioners.
- Weaknesses: The scientific/biological utility of the improvements is not fully established. Virtual screening performance on unseen molecules improves but the margin over the best baseline is moderate (e.g., 19.2→18.5 FID on unseen in Table 2, with KID improvements). Without downstream task validation (e.g., MOA retrieval, dose-response trends, or morphology embedding consistency), it is unclear how much better these models are for the actual decision-making workflows beyond image realism.

Originality:
- Strengths: The main novelty is not a new generative objective but a systematic design-space study, plus a domain-adapted transformer stabilization (“MiT”) and large-scale pretraining applied to microscopy flow matching. The counterfactual vs generation-mode comparison with a single training setup is a useful angle.
- Weaknesses: Several components are adaptations of existing diffusion/DiT practices (conditioning dropout/CFG, transformer scaling, skip connections/dropout/norm tweaks). The contribution is primarily empirical synthesis and scaling rather than fundamentally new modeling.

Overall, this is a strong experimental paper with clear improvements on standard microscopy generative benchmarks and good reproducibility, but the evaluation remains heavily centered on FID/KID and the theoretical section provides limited actionable insight beyond a framing.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) For BBBC021 unseen-molecule conditioning: exactly which parameters are updated during adaptor training (only the 100M adaptor, or also the base model’s AdaLN modulation layers as stated)? Can you provide an ablation showing unseen FID/KID when (a) adaptor-only is trained vs (b) adaptor+AdaLN vs (c) full finetuning, to clarify what drives the gains?

2) Can you add a perturbation-specific fidelity evaluation beyond FID/KID that tests whether the generated distribution preserves biological signal (e.g., agreement in a pretrained morphology embedding space between real and generated per-perturbation distributions; or MOA classification using embeddings extracted from real vs generated)? This would address whether improvements are largely marginal realism.

3) How sensitive are the RxRx1 conclusions (N→D beats C→P; OT not helpful; interpolant choice) to the evaluation protocol (RGB projection, held-out 100-perturbation validation subset, and the small number of controls)? Do the same conclusions hold if you evaluate on a broader perturbation set or alternative splits (even as an additional appendix experiment)?

4) For pretraining on Phenoprints: can you report quantitative pretraining/finetuning curves (FID/KID vs steps) and an ablation on whether the modest RxRx1 gain from pretraining is due to benchmark saturation vs suboptimal transfer (e.g., mismatch in channels, cell type, perturbation distribution, or conditioning schema)?

5) Counterfactual sampling: you observe worse FID but better KID in some cases. Can you clarify the intended use-case and whether counterfactual mode improves any perturbation-effect metric (e.g., estimated treatment effect maps, preservation of non-perturbation features) in a way that is measurable beyond the qualitative figure?
review.limitations: No. The “Impact Statement” explicitly says no societal consequences need to be highlighted, which is not adequate given the application area (drug discovery/biology). The paper should (i) discuss limitations of FID/KID for scientific validity and risks of over-optimizing for perceptual realism, (ii) address dataset biases/batch effects and whether models may amplify artifacts or confounders, (iii) clarify that generated phenotypes are not experimental evidence and could mislead screening decisions, and (iv) comment on dual-use or misuse risks (e.g., inappropriate claims of causal effects from counterfactual generation) and recommended safeguards/validation steps before real-world use.

title: HyperMLP: An Integrated Perspective for Sequence Modeling

review.summary:
The paper reframes an autoregressive self-attention head as a context-instantiated depth-2 MLP whose hidden width grows with sequence length: the “attention score” vector is treated as a hidden pre-activation, and the head output is a gated/activated readout from a context-instantiated memory pool rather than a probability-weighted expectation.

Building on this perspective, the authors propose HyperMLP (and a gated variant HyperGLU) that augment this dynamic-MLP form by (i) learning explicit mixing in the sequence/hidden (length-t) dimension via input-conditioned diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) operators, (ii) also allowing input-conditioned feature-space mixing via low-rank factors and diagonal gating, and (iii) using a reverse-offset “lag” layout so that the canonical extension of the sequence mixing operators aligns with autoregressive truncation/extension semantics. The paper provides theoretical characterizations of the induced memory/pool/activation interpretation, routing geometry (polyhedral vs warped partitions), extension-consistency with the lag layout, and rank/budget allocation arguments. Empirically, it reports controlled ablations on MAD and NanoGPT OpenWebText2, and larger-scale language modeling at 340M/15B tokens and 1.3B/100B tokens with an Open LLM Leaderboard-style evaluation suite, showing improvements over softmax attention and several alternative sequence models under matched parameter budgets.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness (good):
- The core algebraic observation (rewriting attention as a two-layer dynamic map with context-instantiated matrices) is clearly derived, and the paper is careful about what changes when replacing softmax with ReLU◦(scalar) L2 normalization (gate/sign invariance). The memory-pool measure formulation is consistent with the model equations and helps formalize the “pool → activated” interpretation.
- The lag-layout justification is one of the strongest technical pieces: Theorem 2.3 / Appendix F.1 formalize a precise extension-consistency condition and show why the reverse-offset indexing makes the canonical top-left extension correspond to AR truncation invariance.
- Theoretical claims about routing geometry (static → hyperplane arrangements; dynamic R(x) → curved level sets) are plausible and supported by standard arguments (implicit function theorem / differentials).
- Main potential soundness gaps: (i) several “design principle explanations” (e.g., LoRA placement, QK vs VO compression) are argued via simplified residual-MLP rank statements; while correct as linear-algebra facts, the connection to full transformer behavior is suggestive rather than fully validated within the paper. (ii) The parameter-budget matching strategy reallocates capacity in a somewhat bespoke way (e.g., adding extra gating M(2)(x) “costs” a d^2 term); the precise accounting per architecture is hard to audit from the paper alone without a detailed per-block parameter table for all baselines.

Presentation (good):
- The paper is unusually thorough: clear notation, multiple complementary views (dynamic-MLP, memory measures, geometry), and extensive appendix map.
- Figures (esp. attention-as-MLP decomposition and lag/DPLR implementation sketches) help.
- Weakness: the model definition is dense and introduces many moving parts (L(1)/L(2), R(1)/R(2), M(1)/M(2), S(j), DPLR, conv option, lag layout). While the labeling scheme in Table 1 helps, a single “default HyperGLU block” pseudocode and a concise parameter/FLOP breakdown for every compared method would improve accessibility and auditability.

Significance (good):
- If the reported matched-budget gains hold broadly, learned sequence-axis mixing inside attention-like blocks could be a meaningful direction for improving capability per parameter/compute while preserving AR usability.
- The work also contributes a coherent conceptual lens that can unify many attention variants.
- However, the practical impact is tempered by (i) inability to use highly optimized kernels like FlashAttention, (ii) the need to fix nhead=2 for cost reasons, and (iii) limited scaling evidence beyond 1.3B params / 100B tokens. The paper acknowledges some of these.

Originality (good):
- The “attention as dynamic two-layer MLP” viewpoint is not entirely unprecedented in spirit, but the paper’s integrated framing plus the specific HyperMLP design (input-conditioned DPLR mixing on the sequence dimension + lag layout with extension-consistency analysis + GLU decoupling of routing vs magnitude) feels novel as a combined package.
- The lag-layout formalization in particular is a distinctive contribution.

Empirical strengths:
- Controlled design study (Table 1) is well structured: ablations isolate softmax vs ReLU normalization, feature modifiers (RoPE/conv/gates), QK vs VO compression, presence/placement of temporal mixing, and the lag layout effect. The “without lag collapses” result is striking and aligns with the theory.
- Larger-scale LM results (Table 2) show consistent improvements of HyperMLP/HyperGLU over softmax attention and several sequence-model baselines under the paper’s training protocol.

Empirical weaknesses / missing checks:
- The paper’s strongest claims are “consistently outperform under matched parameter budgets”; but the matching depends on architectural choices (notably head count changes and rank reallocations). It is not fully transparent how sensitive results are to these choices (e.g., what happens if attention is also forced to nhead=2; or if HyperMLP is allowed more heads but smaller per-head ranks).
- Variance/reproducibility is unclear: the controlled study appears to report single runs; no error bars or multiple seeds are provided.
- It would help to see standard perplexity on held-out validation for the NanoGPT experiment rather than training-subset loss and “steps to reach thresholds,” which can be noisy and sensitive to evaluation protocol.
- Since the method changes the attention operator substantially, it would be useful to report downstream latency/throughput in the main text (Table 5 is in the appendix) and clarify which numbers include compilation/warmup and whether kernels are comparable across baselines.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Parameter matching: Can you provide a per-block (or per-layer) parameter breakdown for each main baseline in Tables 1–2 (SoftmaxAttn(+mods), ReLUAttn(+mods), HyperMLP, HyperGLU), including how changing nhead (e.g., Hyper* fixed at 2) affects total params and whether any hidden dimension or MLP sizes were adjusted? This directly affects how I interpret “matched budget.”

2) Statistical reliability: For the controlled design study (MAD + NanoGPT), how many random seeds were run per configuration? If only one, can you report variance over (say) 3 seeds for the key comparisons (e.g., R-cg-q vs R-cg-q-12o; G-cg-q-12o vs best softmax baseline)?
