- Strengths: The paper is generally well structured: problem setup, method, theory, experiments, and limitations. The time-advance block is specified with concrete equations (ETD + ϕ1 forcing + masking) and explicit “knobs” αg, αw, L. Experimental protocol follows APEBench and reports the benchmark aggregate metric plus stability-step CDFs on selected tasks.
- Weaknesses: Some experimental details are hard to reconcile: Table 1 includes a baseline “Dil” and uses “UNet”/“Res”/“Conv” but the paper does not describe these baselines’ architectures or ensure parameter/compute matching beyond one micro-benchmark against FNO on 1D Burgers. The “strongest baseline” in the stability plots is referred to as “Dil” with a specific configuration string, but that mapping is not described in the main text. Also, the paper claims ablations confirm roles of “generator constraint, gating, and filtering,” but the shown ablations (Table 2) only toggle αg and αw; there is no direct ablation of the Re(λ) constraint vs unconstrained generator, nor a systematic ablation of mask/truncation.

Significance:
- Strengths: Long-horizon stability is a central pain point for autoregressive neural PDE surrogates; a stepper-level design that incorporates ETD structure and explicit non-expansive linear dynamics is potentially useful and broadly applicable. The reported gains on a standardized benchmark suite (APEBench) across 1D/2D/3D tasks are substantial on several scenarios.
- Weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is limited to 7 tasks (a subset of the benchmark), with fixed resolution/time step and only modest stress testing on a single 2D task. It is therefore uncertain how robust the improvements are across broader PDE families, varying stiffness, or distribution shifts. The largest gains appear on some tasks (e.g., Dispersion-1D and KdV-1D), but one task (SwiftH-3D) is not best, and Kolmogorov-2D improvements are relatively smaller; more analysis would be needed to establish when SGNO is preferable.

Originality:
- Strengths: The specific combination of (i) a learned diagonal Fourier generator used in an ETD update with an explicit nonpositive real-part parameterization, plus (ii) applying spectral masking/truncation only to the ETD forcing term (not to the full state), and (iii) per-mode channel mixing, is a reasonably distinct design point and is backed by an architecture-aligned bound.
- Weaknesses: Many components are incremental variations on existing Fourier-operator + stabilization ideas (spectral truncation, masking, ETD/integrating-factor-like updates, gain control), and the diagonal-generator restriction may limit expressivity compared to more general linear operators; the paper does not deeply justify this tradeoff or compare to a variant with non-diagonal linear mixing in the propagator.

Overall, the paper has a clear motivation and promising empirical results, but the evaluation/ablations do not fully isolate which components drive improvements (constraint vs filtering vs ETD form), and the theoretical analysis is not connected to measurable quantities in the experiments.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Generator constraint ablation: What happens if you remove the constraint Re(λ)≤0 (i.e., allow α to be unconstrained or positive) while keeping all else fixed? Does long-horizon stability degrade in a way consistent with the theory?
2) Filtering/truncation contribution: Can you provide ablations for (a) no truncation / more modes, (b) mask on/off (and different γ,p), and crucially (c) applying the same filter to the full state vs only to the forcing pathway? This is important to justify the design choice that filtering the forcing is the key stabilizer.
3) Baseline comparability: What are the exact definitions/architectures of Conv/Res/UNet/Dil baselines and how are their parameter counts and compute matched to SGNO across 1D/2D/3D? Are the reported numbers from official APEBench baselines or your reimplementations?
4) Stability metrics across all tasks: Beyond the two qualitative stability plots, can you report stable-step statistics (e.g., median and IQR at τ=0.2 or task-specific τ) for all seven tasks and the main competing baselines to corroborate “longer stable rollout lengths”?
5) Practical link to theory: Did you measure/estimate any of the quantities appearing in q(δt) (e.g., spectral norms of Mθ(k), empirical Lipschitz estimates of G/W, or observed feature norms) to verify whether q(δt) is plausibly ≤1 or to diagnose when/why instability occurs?
review.limitations: yes. The paper includes a limitations section that correctly notes: (i) evaluation on only a subset of APEBench and mostly fixed ∆t/resolution; (ii) the theory is local and not an end-to-end certificate because nonlinear Lipschitz/mixing bounds are not enforced/reported; and (iii) use of first-order ETD Euler and limited ablations. The paper could further discuss potential failure modes under non-periodic boundary conditions (since the method is built around Fourier structure) and clarify any negative societal impact (likely minimal here) primarily around misuse/overtrust of long-horizon surrogates without calibrated uncertainty.

title: KVSlimmer: Theoretical Insights and Practical Optimizations for Asymmetric KV Merging

review.summary:
This paper studies KV-cache merging for long-context LLM inference, motivated by the empirical “asymmetry” that adjacent Keys are often similar while adjacent Values remain diverse. The authors first propose a spectral-view explanation: cosine similarity between adjacent projected tokens can be decomposed into contributions from spectral modes of the projection matrix, and concentrated spectra (as observed for W_Q and W_K) lead to higher adjacent similarity, while more dispersed spectra (as observed for W_V) preserve heterogeneity.

Building on this, the paper introduces KVSlimmer, an asymmetric KV merging method that (i) derives an exact second-order Hessian block structure for attention logits with respect to Keys, including off-diagonal key–key coupling terms, and (ii) removes the need for backpropagation at inference by converting the Hessian-based optimal merged-key solution into a closed-form weight rule depending only on forward-pass quantities (attention weights, values, and head output). The method is evaluated on LongBench and LongBenchV2 across several instruction-tuned models, reporting improved accuracy over prior merging/eviction/segmentation baselines and lower runtime and peak memory than AsymKV, especially for larger chunk sizes.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The paper provides a clear mathematical derivation of the key gradients and Hessian blocks for softmax attention (Eqs. 12–22). A notable result is that each Hessian block is rank-one (scaled qq^T), and the off-diagonal coupling term is explicit (Eq. 22), addressing a concrete limitation claimed for AsymKV.
- Weaknesses: The core step that enables “gradient-free” merging relies on an empirical alignment relation cos(E,c11)≈cos(E,c22)≈−cos(E,c12) (Eq. 32). While the appendix offers intuition based on near-convergence stability and softmax sign structure, the argument is qualitative and not a theorem with explicit conditions. Since Eq. 33 (the final closed-form weights) depends critically on this approximation, it is unclear how robust the method is when the relation fails (e.g., different prompts, distribution shift, early layers, or atypical attention regimes). Additionally, Eq. 29 notes the solution lies in span{q} and then “equivalently” expresses it in span{km,km+1} to cancel qq^T; this equivalence is not fully justified in the text (it may hold only for the particular linear system structure / pseudoinverse choice). A more rigorous statement of when Eq. 30–33 are guaranteed to match the original Hessian optimum would strengthen correctness.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well structured: it motivates gaps in AsymKV, introduces a spectral analysis, then develops the Hessian and simplification. Figures and tables are readable and the experimental setup is mostly clear (budgets, chunk size, hardware).
- Weaknesses: Some key implementation and algorithmic details are missing or only implicit: e.g., the exact rule for selecting which adjacent pairs to merge within each chunk/budget (is it the same as AsymKV’s criterion? based on attention mass, similarity, or fixed pairing?), and how Eq. 33 is applied per head/layer across steps. Without a precise algorithm box/pseudocode, reproducibility and understanding of the method’s behavior are reduced. The “Impact Statement” is generic and does not discuss plausible impacts.

Significance:
- Strengths: KV-cache compression is practically important for long-context inference. The reported gains include both quality improvements over a strong baseline (AsymKV) and substantial latency/memory reductions, especially at larger chunk sizes where AsymKV becomes expensive or OOM. If robust, a gradient-free second-order merging rule could be broadly useful.
- Weaknesses: Accuracy improvements over AsymKV on LongBench averages are modest (e.g., +0.92, +0.40, +0.47 depending on model). The paper does not show statistical variability (seeds, confidence intervals), so it is hard to gauge significance of small deltas.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of (i) an explicit exact Hessian derivation including off-diagonal coupling and (ii) a forward-only closed-form merging weight rule is a clear conceptual advance over gradient-based approximations. The spectral-energy explanation for Q/K vs V similarity provides a coherent lens connecting weight spectra to token-level (dis)similarity.
- Weaknesses: The spectral analysis is primarily explanatory/diagnostic and supported empirically; its novelty is moderate relative to being an application of SVD-based reasoning to cosine similarity. The main algorithmic novelty rests on the gradient-elimination approximation (Eq. 32), which is empirically motivated.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Algorithm specification: What is the exact procedure for choosing which adjacent key pairs to merge within a chunk/budget (pairing pattern, scoring/selection, per-head vs averaged), and is it identical to AsymKV’s selection mechanism? Please provide pseudocode.

2) Robustness of Eq. (32): How often (quantitatively) does cos(E,c11)≈cos(E,c22)≈−cos(E,c12) hold across layers, heads, tasks, and models? What is the distribution of approximation error, and how does performance degrade if this relation is violated?

3) Exactness vs approximation: In what precise sense does KVSlimmer “retain exact Hessian information” while also being gradient-free? Is Eq. (33) exactly equivalent to the Hessian-optimal solution under stated assumptions, or is it an approximation? Please state the assumptions/conditions formally.

4) Pairwise merge stability: Eq. (33) involves a denominator (||c11||^2 − 2||c12||^2 + ||c22||^2). How often is this near-zero or negative in practice, and what safeguards are implemented (clipping, fallback to uniform weights, skipping merges)?

5) Statistical reliability: Are the LongBench/LongBenchV2 improvements averaged over multiple runs/seeds? If not, can you report variance or confidence intervals, especially for the small average gains over AsymKV?
review.limitations: No. The limitations section discusses only technical extensions (non-local merging; adaptive per-layer ratios). It should also address: (i) reliance on the empirical alignment assumption (Eq. 32) and when it may fail, (ii) potential failure modes under distribution shift or different fine-tuning stages, (iii) numerical stability concerns in Eq. 33, and (iv) potential societal impacts of enabling cheaper long-context inference (e.g., scaling up deployment, privacy concerns with longer retained context, and misuse amplification), even if the risks are indirect.

title: Solving the Offline and Online Min-Max Problem of Non-smooth Submodular-Concave Functions: A Zeroth-Order Approach

review.summary: The paper studies mixed discrete–continuous max–min / min–max optimization where the discrete decision is a subset S of a ground set and the continuous decision is y in a compact convex set. The objective f(S,y) is assumed submodular in S and concave (possibly non-smooth) in y. The authors leverage the Lovász extension to relax submodular minimization over sets into convex minimization over the hypercube, yielding a (generally non-smooth) convex–concave saddle-point problem in variables (x,y). They propose a zeroth-order extragradient (ZO-EG) algorithm: use a computable subgradient of the Lovász extension w.r.t. x (requiring only function evaluations) and a two-point Gaussian-smoothing gradient estimator w.r.t. y. For the offline setting, they provide expected convergence bounds to an ε-saddle point with explicit step-size/smoothing choices and a function-query complexity scaling as O(ε^{-2}) (with dimension dependence through m). For the online setting with time-varying fk, they extend the analysis to bound expected online (duality/restricted) gap in terms of the path length of an optimal solution sequence, obtaining an O(sqrt(N\bar P_N)) style bound. The theory is illustrated on synthetic adversarial semi-supervised image segmentation and clustering examples, with a comparison to U-Net baselines in an online segmentation setup.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The reduction via the Lovász extension and the use of extragradient with (i) exact subgradients in x (computed from function values through the Lovász chain construction) and (ii) Gaussian-smoothing gradient estimates in y is coherent. Theorems 3.2 and 3.5 state explicit expected bounds, and the appendices provide proof sketches that follow a standard projection/non-expansiveness + telescoping argument, plus a smoothing bias term.
- Weaknesses: The main guarantees for the original discrete problem (over S) rely on a nontrivial assumption: existence of a saddle point for f and/or an integrality condition (Eq. (10)) ensuring the relaxation matches the discrete min–max. While Propositions 2.10–2.11 discuss conditions, the algorithm and theorems effectively assume away the potentially large integrality/saddle-point gap; the offline theorem ultimately bounds a quantity involving E_\tau[f(S_\tau, y)] (threshold rounding) rather than the actual max_y f(S,y) for the returned discrete S. This makes the strength of the guarantee for (1) somewhat indirect.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well organized (problem → preliminaries → algorithm → offline/online theorems → experiments). Key objects (duality gap, restricted gap, Lovász extension, smoothing) are defined.
- Weaknesses: There are several points where notation and claims are easy to misinterpret: (i) the paper alternates between guarantees for f, f^L, and a thresholded/expected version D_\tau; it is not always clearly stated what final output is for the original discrete saddle definition and what metric it optimizes; (ii) the computational model (number of value-oracle calls per iteration) is discussed only briefly and inconsistently—computing gx via (8) requires multiple f evaluations through chain values, while evaluating f^L(x,y+\mu u) may itself require multiple f calls; (iii) the experiments compare to U-Nets but do not specify several key experimental details needed for a fair comparison (training procedure specifics, compute budget parity, adversary strength on baselines).

Significance:
- Strengths: Addressing min–max problems with a submodular–concave structure in both offline and online regimes, under derivative-free access for the continuous player, is a meaningful niche combining combinatorial optimization, saddle-point methods, and online learning. The online path-length dependence is potentially useful for tracking non-stationary equilibria.
- Weaknesses: The practical impact is limited by (a) the strong assumption that a saddle point for the original discrete game exists and aligns with the Lovász relaxation, and (b) the dimension dependence and oracle complexity are not fully transparent in terms of real function-query costs for large n. The empirical section is synthetic and task-specific; broader evidence of utility is limited.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of Lovász-extension subgradients (for the discrete/submodular side) with Gaussian-smoothing ZO estimates (for the continuous concave side) inside an extragradient framework, plus an online analysis with path-length, appears novel within the scope framed by the paper.
- Weaknesses: Algorithmically, the components (Lovász-extension subgradients; Gaussian smoothing; extragradient) are standard building blocks; the novelty is primarily in tailoring them to this mixed submodular–concave min–max setting and providing the accompanying analysis.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Discrete vs relaxed guarantee: Theorems bound quantities for f^L and for D_\tau(S,y)=max_y E_\tau[f(S_\tau,y)]-min_S f(S,y). How does this translate into a bound on the original duality gap max_y f(S,y)-min_S f(S,ȳ) for the returned discrete S (without expectation over τ)? Is there a rounding/selection step that yields a comparable guarantee for the true discrete objective?
2) Saddle-point existence / integrality: Your main results assume a saddle point for (1) exists and often rely on Eq. (10)-type conditions. In your target applications (segmentation/clustering), can you justify that these conditions hold (or quantify the potential integrality/saddle-point gap)?
3) Oracle/query complexity accounting: What is the exact number of value-oracle calls to f per iteration as a function of n, t_k, and the need to evaluate f^L (which itself may require multiple f evaluations)? The paper states O(m^2 ε^{-2}) function queries; does this count calls to f(S,y) or to f^L(x,y), and how does the n-dependence enter?
4) Non-smoothness in y: The algorithm uses Gaussian smoothing to obtain ∇_y f^L_μ, but the function is only assumed Lipschitz in y. Are there additional assumptions needed to ensure the stated variance bound Eu[||g_μ||^2] ≤ L_{0y}^2 (m+4)^2 used in the proofs when f^L is non-smooth in y?
5) Online setting definition: Theorem 3.5 uses path length of z̄_k defined via best responses to (x̂_k,ŷ_k). Is P̄_N assumed known for step-size selection? If not, how should h2 be chosen adaptively, and do the guarantees still hold?
review.limitations: No. The paper does not meaningfully discuss limitations or potential negative societal impacts. Suggested additions: (i) explicitly discuss the strong assumptions required for discrete saddle-point existence / integrality and how violations affect guarantees; (ii) provide a clear accounting of oracle complexity in n and discuss scalability; (iii) discuss robustness claims carefully—“robust by design” depends on the adversary model (budget set Y_ρ) and may not extend to other perturbations; (iv) address potential misuse in adversarial settings (e.g., optimizing worst-case objectives could be used to design attacks) and dataset/benchmark limitations of the experiments.

title: Grounding Generated Videos in Feasible Plans via World Models

review.summary:
The paper studies how to turn video-generated “plans” (image-to-video rollouts conditioned on start/goal) into executable actions when the generated videos are temporally inconsistent or physically infeasible. It proposes GVP-WM, a test-time planning method that uses a pretrained action-conditioned world model to “project” a video plan onto dynamically feasible trajectories.

Concretely, the method encodes the generated video frames into the world model’s latent space, then solves a constrained latent trajectory optimization problem via direct latent collocation: latent states and actions are jointly optimized while enforcing world-model dynamics as constraints. Video guidance enters as (i) initialization of latent knot points from the encoded video and (ii) a scale-invariant (cosine/normalized) latent alignment loss, plus a terminal goal loss. The constrained problem is solved with an augmented Lagrangian approach, and the resulting actions are executed with MPC (optionally with local sampling refinement).

Experiments on two 2D simulation tasks (Push-T manipulation and Wall navigation) compare against MPC with CEM and gradient descent (no video guidance) and a video-to-action inverse-dynamics baseline (UniPi) under different sources/qualities of video plans: zero-shot I2V, LoRA-finetuned I2V, oracle expert videos, and motion-blurred variants. The paper reports success rates, planning time, qualitative examples, and ablations isolating initialization, alignment loss, collocation, MPC, and the scale-invariant alignment choice.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The formulation is clear: a constrained optimization in latent space with explicit dynamics constraints (via f_\psi) and explicit decision variables for both latent states and actions (collocation). The use of augmented Lagrangian to handle nonlinear equality constraints is appropriate, and the algorithmic steps (initialization from video latents, primal/dual updates, penalty schedule) are described at a high level.
- Weaknesses: Several key technical details needed to assess correctness/reproducibility are underspecified in the main text: handling of history H in the constraints (boundary conditions for t < H), how the initial segment z_{t-H:t} and a_{t-H:t} are treated inside MPC, and how gradients are computed through the encoder/normalization (e.g., whether z variables are unconstrained latent vectors independent of E_\phi except at initialization). In addition, success rates are given without any measure of variance/uncertainty across seeds or optimization randomness (ALM initialization, Adam, local refinement sampling). Finally, the comparison to UniPi is constrained to “same video plans”, but UniPi’s training/setup is not detailed in the main text (only referenced), making it hard to judge fairness beyond the input videos.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well organized (problem → method → optimization → MPC execution → experiments). Equations (3–5) and Algorithm 1 make the method understandable. The qualitative figures directly illustrate the failure modes (teleportation, blur, drift) and the claimed recovery behavior.
- Weaknesses: Some claims are hard to verify due to missing quantitative diagnostics: there is no reporting of constraint satisfaction (e.g., ||L_dyn||) at convergence, no breakdown of failure causes (world-model mismatch vs. video mismatch vs. optimization failure), and the computational budget for baselines (e.g., number of CEM samples/iterations) is not fully spelled out in the main body.

Significance:
- Strengths: The paper tackles a practical and timely gap between “video as plan” and “actions that work”, proposing an inference-time grounding method that does not require additional environment interaction or training. The improvements over inverse-dynamics execution under severe temporal blur are large, and the oracle-video setting suggests potential when video guidance is reliable.
- Weaknesses: Evidence is limited to two 2D simulated domains with a specific pretrained world model and a single I2V generator; generality to higher-dimensional/real robotics is argued but not demonstrated. Also, in the hardest/most realistic case highlighted by the paper—zero-shot I2V guidance that is strongly OOD—GVP-WM can underperform unguided MPC-CEM in several settings, indicating the method’s benefit depends materially on guidance quality and/or video finetuning.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of (i) video-plan latent encoding, (ii) explicit collocation over latent states (not just actions), and (iii) a scale-invariant alignment objective as soft guidance while enforcing dynamics constraints is a coherent and reasonably novel integration aimed specifically at “grounding” infeasible video plans.
- Weaknesses: Conceptually it is an incremental extension of latent collocation/planning in world models by adding an extra guidance term and initialization from a video model. The novelty thus relies on demonstrating that this particular integration materially improves robustness to infeasible video artifacts, which is partially supported but still limited by scope of tasks.

Overall, the work is technically plausible and empirically promising, but the experimental scope and some missing implementation/analysis details limit how strongly one can conclude general effectiveness and robustness.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Constraint handling/details: How exactly are the dynamics constraints implemented for timesteps near the beginning of the horizon given the history length H (e.g., for t < H)? Are missing past latents/actions padded, copied from the current state, or optimized as additional variables? This affects feasibility and fairness across horizons.

2) Optimization reliability: What fraction of failures are due to ALM/Adam not converging (e.g., large remaining ||L_dyn||) versus converging to a feasible-but-bad plan? Can you report average/max dynamics violation at the end of optimization and correlate it with success?

3) Baseline compute parity: What are the exact CEM settings (population size, elites, iterations) and GD settings (steps, lr, restarts) used for MPC-CEM/MPC-GD, and were they tuned under the same validation protocol/budget as GVP-WM? Table 2 suggests large time differences; it would be important to know if baselines were given comparable wall-clock budgets.

4) UniPi comparability: How is UniPi trained for Push-T and Wall in your experiments (dataset size, action/state definitions, frame subsampling), and does it have access to proprioception or only images? Since UniPi is a major baseline, these details could change the interpretation of the large gaps under blurred guidance.

5) Sensitivity to guidance weight: How sensitive is performance to λ_v across WAN-0S vs WAN-FT? The ablation suggests guidance can hurt under WAN-0S; is there an automatic mechanism (e.g., detect misalignment and downweight) that could avoid regressions relative to unguided planning? If not, how often does guidance harm in practice?
review.limitations:
Partially. The paper includes a limitations section noting dependence on world-model accuracy, remaining test-time optimization cost, and that severely misaligned zero-shot guidance can hurt relative to unguided planning. However, the “Impact Statement” appears empty, and the paper does not meaningfully discuss potential negative societal impacts or misuse (e.g., stronger planning/control from generated video could be applied in safety-critical settings; reliance on pretrained large models and dataset biases).

Suggestions: (i) add a brief impact statement addressing safety considerations of executing plans derived from generative models, especially under model mismatch; (ii) discuss failure detection/uncertainty estimation and safe fallback (e.g., switching to unguided MPC when guidance is inconsistent); (iii) discuss compute/energy costs given the use of a 14B video model plus iterative optimization.

title: UAOR: Uncertainty-aware Observation Reinjection for Vision-Language-Action Models

review.summary: The paper proposes UAOR (Uncertainty-aware Observation Reinjection), a training-free plug-in module for vision-language-action (VLA) transformer policies. UAOR monitors per-layer “action uncertainty” during inference using an action-entropy metric computed from intermediate layer logits (via a logit-lens style LM-head projection on action/condition tokens). When uncertainty at layer \(\ell\) exceeds a threshold \(\gamma\), the method reinjects observation features (visual and optionally proprioceptive tokens) into the subsequent layer’s FFN output via an attention-like key-value retrieval over observation tokens, mixed with the original FFN output using a blending factor \(\alpha\). The paper provides an information-theoretic analysis (mutual information increase, conditional entropy reduction, and an information-bottleneck objective argument) and evaluates UAOR on multiple simulators (LIBERO, SIMPLER, CALVIN) and on real-robot tasks, reporting consistent success-rate improvements with small inference overhead. Ablations examine injection mechanism, retrieval vs mean pooling, trigger policies, what modalities to reinject, hyperparameter sensitivity, and injection timing/location (FFN vs self-attention; current vs next layer).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The method is clearly specified (Eqs. 6–9, Algorithm 1) and the engineering choices are validated with targeted ablations (Table 4, Table 5, Table 10). The comparison across heterogeneous VLA architectures (single-system vs dual-system; discrete/continuous action heads) supports the claim of being a plug-in inference-time module. The timing/location ablation (Table 10) directly supports the “next-layer FFN” design choice with a latency/performance tradeoff.
- Weaknesses: The core uncertainty metric (Action Entropy) relies on projecting intermediate hidden states through the LM head and using a top-K categorical distribution (Eq. 6). For continuous-action models, the paper fixes K=256 “for definitional convenience,” but does not justify why entropy computed from a token distribution in LM vocabulary space is a faithful proxy for action uncertainty in those settings; similarly, for π0 and CogACT the entropy is computed on a single condition/prefix token (Na=1), which seems only indirectly connected to action uncertainty. The theoretical analysis hinges on assumptions like “near-invertible mixing” and correlation assumptions in Theorem 3.4; while reasonable as intuition, these are not empirically validated (e.g., measuring correlation between u^(ℓ) and downstream failure or entropy) beyond qualitative references to Figures 1–2.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is well organized, with a concrete algorithm, clear figures illustrating uncertainty/attention decay, and extensive appendices documenting baselines, hyperparameters, and additional ablations. Tables report mean±std over seeds for key simulation results.
- Weaknesses: Some claims are stated broadly without sufficient qualification (e.g., “observation forgetting” as the cause of uncertainty rise), and the “Impact Statements” section is essentially non-informative. Also, the method depends on hyperparameters (γ, α) that are tuned per task/suite/model (Table 7); the presentation could more clearly separate what is fixed vs tuned and how much tuning is needed in a new deployment.

Significance:
- Strengths: A training-free, plug-and-play inference modification that yields consistent gains on strong VLA baselines (including near-saturated LIBERO numbers) is practically relevant. The real-robot improvements reported are sizable (e.g., OpenVLA-OFT average 55.0→72.5; CogACT 63.8→78.8), and overhead is small (~5% latency on LIBERO-Long).
- Weaknesses: Many simulation gains are modest in absolute terms (often ~+1 point on already high success rates), which raises questions about how often the method meaningfully changes behavior in less-saturated regimes. The real-world evaluation uses per-task fine-tuning on 50 trajectories; it is unclear whether UAOR helps in a truly “no additional training/data” real-world setting, since the deployed policies are task-adapted.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of (i) layer-wise uncertainty trigger, (ii) reinjection of observation via FFN-key-value retrieval, and (iii) inference-time intervention for VLA models without retraining is a coherent and somewhat distinctive recipe, especially with the detailed ablations around where/when to inject.
- Weaknesses: The reinjection operation (Eq. 9) is essentially an attention-style retrieval over observation tokens, and the “FFN as memory” perspective is used primarily as motivation rather than requiring FFN parameter reuse; the method is closer to adding an extra retrieval/mixing pathway than truly “using the FFN weights as memory.” As a result, the novelty is incremental in mechanism, though still valuable if robustly demonstrated.

Reproducibility notes:
- The paper provides many implementation details (Appendix B) but does not include sufficient procedural detail to exactly reproduce tuning (e.g., how γ is selected from uncertainty curves quantitatively, how many evaluations are used to choose α/γ, and whether tuning uses test tasks).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How is Action Entropy computed for continuous-action models in a way that meaningfully reflects action uncertainty? In particular, when you set K=256 “for definitional convenience,” what are the 256 candidates and how are their probabilities obtained from the LM head if the action head is not discrete-token based?
2) Hyperparameter selection: Are γ and α tuned using the same evaluation episodes used to report final numbers (potential test-set tuning)? Please specify the exact tuning protocol (budget, split, and whether tuning is per-task/suite/model).
3) Can you quantify the claimed correlation that motivates Theorem 3.4 (u^(ℓ) correlates with H(y|h) / failures)? For example, report correlation between layer uncertainty statistics (or trigger frequency) and rollout success or error types across tasks.
4) For dual-system policies (π0/CogACT) you compute entropy on a single token (Na=1). Why is that the right token, and did you compare against alternatives (e.g., averaging over a span of tokens, or using system-1 internal uncertainty if available)?
5) Real-world setting: since you fine-tune baselines on 50 trajectories per task, does UAOR still help (and by how much) when applied to the off-the-shelf pretrained models without task-specific fine-tuning, or under fewer trajectories (e.g., 0/10/20)? This affects the “training-free” practical claim in real deployments.
review.limitations: No. The limitations/impact discussion is not adequate: the Impact Statements section claims no implications to highlight, which is implausible for robotic manipulation policies. The paper should discuss (i) potential safety risks of increased “confidence” (entropy reduction) leading to overconfident unsafe actions, (ii) failure modes when reinjection injects irrelevant or spurious visual features (e.g., clutter, reflective surfaces), (iii) sensitivity to γ/α and distribution shifts (lighting/camera changes), (iv) computational/memory costs for very long context or multi-view tokens, and (v) possible misuse in autonomous systems. Concretely, include an analysis of failure cases and a safety-oriented evaluation (e.g., collision/near-miss metrics or intervention frequency) to complement success rates.

title: When Scaling Fails: Mitigating Audio Perception Decay of LALMs via Multi-Step Perception-Aware Reasoning

review.summary:
The paper studies why test-time scaling via longer explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can give marginal or even negative gains in Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) compared to direct-answer RL tuning. It introduces CAFE, a “LLM-as-a-judge” evaluation framework that extracts audio events from model reasoning traces (using a captioning model to provide a reference) and quantifies (i) perception accuracy/error, (ii) usage error, and (iii) omission error. Using CAFE, the authors report a phenomenon they call “audio perception decay”: as reasoning token length increases, both perceived audio-event fidelity and task accuracy decline for several open-source audio models.

To mitigate this, the paper proposes MPAR^2, a structured “think-while-listening” paradigm with three stages (Perception → multi-step Reasoning via sub-questions → Review). MPAR^2 is trained with a two-stage scheme: SFT on a curated set of synthetic audio-reasoning traces, followed by GRPO reinforcement learning using several generative rewards (perception reward, stepwise perception-reasoning reward, review-enhanced accuracy reward, and a format reward). The resulting Qwen2.5-Omni-based models improve benchmark accuracy (e.g., on MMAU test-mini and MMAR) and substantially increase CAFE perception accuracy while stabilizing performance across longer reasoning lengths; the paper also analyzes attention-to-audio and adaptive reasoning length behavior.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The paper clearly operationalizes “reasoning-time perception” with explicit event categories (matched/hallucinated/misused/missed/neutral) and defines concrete metrics (Acc_per, Err_per, Err_use, Err_omit). The proposed training recipe is well specified (two-stage SFT+GRPO, reward decomposition with equations, ablations), and the empirical results consistently show improvements on both task accuracy and CAFE metrics.
- Weaknesses: The core measurement pipeline depends heavily on a single external judge/captioner (Gemini-3-pro for CAFE; Qwen3-32B for rewards), and the paper provides limited evidence that the extracted event labels/metrics are reliable or robust (e.g., no inter-judge agreement, no sensitivity analysis to caption quality, no human audit). In addition, the “perception decay” claim is supported mainly by correlation of performance vs. token-length bins; it is unclear whether length is causal vs. a proxy for difficulty or uncertainty (harder questions elicit longer traces and lower accuracy), and the analysis does not fully control for this confound.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well organized (problem → evaluation framework → diagnosis → method → experiments → analysis). Figures (perception/accuracy vs length; training schematic; attention ratio; reasoning-length by difficulty) support the narrative, and prompts/reward templates are included in appendices.
- Weaknesses: Several important implementation details for reproducibility are underspecified given the reliance on LLM-judging and synthetic data (e.g., exact CAFE extraction prompts are provided, but not calibration/validation; details on how “reasoning token length intervals” are formed; how many samples per bin; which datasets/questions were used for Figure 3). The “Impact Statement” is cursory and does not engage with plausible misuse or failure modes.

Significance:
- Strengths: The paper targets an important practical issue for audio multimodal reasoning—why longer explicit reasoning may degrade performance—and proposes both a diagnostic tool (CAFE) and a training approach (MPAR^2) that appears to improve perception grounding and overall QA accuracy. The reported jump in CAFE perception accuracy (31.74%→63.51%) is large, and the method improves multiple benchmarks and model sizes (3B and 7B).
- Weaknesses: The overall benchmark gains on MMAR are moderate (e.g., 55.20%→60.32%), and MPAR^2 does not achieve best reported MMAR accuracy among compared systems in Table 2 (e.g., Step-Audio-R1.1/Step-Audio-R1, Audio-Thinker are higher). The broader utility of CAFE beyond the presented setup is uncertain because it requires strong captioning/judging models and access to reasoning traces.

Originality:
- Strengths: Framing the failure of test-time scaling in LALMs as a “perception decay” bottleneck and proposing an explicit Perception→Reasoning→Review pipeline with reward shaping targeted at perception/usage is a coherent and somewhat distinctive angle compared to generic CoT RL.
- Weaknesses: The method largely combines known ingredients (structured prompting, decomposition, review/self-check, GRPO-style RL, LLM-as-judge rewards). The main novelty rests on the specific diagnosis (perception decay) and the particular reward decomposition, but the paper could more sharply delineate what is fundamentally new vs. a tailored application of established tools.

Overall, the work is promising and empirically strong, but the soundness of the central diagnosis and of the CAFE measurements would be substantially strengthened by robustness checks and controls for confounds (difficulty vs. length; caption/judge dependence).
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How do you control for the confound that longer reasoning traces may correspond to harder questions (or lower confidence), rather than length itself causing “perception decay”? For example, do you observe decay when conditioning on question difficulty (MMAR level), or when forcing different reasoning lengths on the same set of questions?

2) How reliable is CAFE’s event extraction and categorization? Can you provide (even on a small subset) human validation, inter-run stability, or cross-judge comparisons (e.g., different textual judges, or captioner vs. non-captioner) to show that Acc_per/Err_* correlate with real perception/usage errors?

3) CAFE uses Gemini-3-pro captions as “ground truth audio caption.” How sensitive are results to caption quality/errors? If the caption misses an event or mislabels it, CAFE may penalize correct model behavior. Do you have an estimate of caption accuracy, or mitigation (e.g., multiple captions, uncertainty)?

4) MPAR^2 training relies on Qwen3-32B as the scoring model S for multiple rewards. What prevents reward hacking (e.g., producing perception text that matches typical caption style) rather than improved audio grounding? Do you have evidence that improvements persist under alternative judges or under human evaluation?

5) The paper reports that commercial models do not show decay while open models do (Figure 3). Are these comparisons controlled for prompt format, maximum tokens, and decoding parameters? Could prompt-induced verbosity differences explain some of the observed trend?
review.limitations: No. The limitations/impact discussion is not adequate. The impact statement is essentially empty, and key methodological limitations are not discussed. The paper should explicitly acknowledge: (i) dependence on proprietary caption/judge models in CAFE (Gemini-3-pro) and potential bias/errors from them; (ii) risk of reward hacking and judge overfitting due to LLM-based rewards; (iii) potential confounding between reasoning length and task difficulty in the “decay” analysis; (iv) additional compute and latency costs introduced by multi-stage reasoning; and (v) societal risks from improved audio understanding (e.g., surveillance, privacy) and how the authors mitigate or at least contextualize them.

title: Quantized Evolution Strategies: High-precision Fine-tuning of Quantized LLMs at Low-precision Cost

review.summary: The paper studies how to fine-tune post-training-quantized (PTQ) LLMs when weights are discrete (e.g., INT4/INT8) and backpropagation-based methods are impractical due to non-differentiability and memory overhead. It proposes Quantized Evolution Strategies (QES), a zeroth-order/evolution-strategies fine-tuning approach that operates directly on quantized integer weights. The core idea is to (i) apply an accumulated error-feedback (residual accumulation) mechanism so that sub-grid updates are not lost to rounding, yielding a “virtual” high-precision trajectory while updating discrete weights, and (ii) avoid storing the dense residual vector by “stateless seed replay,” which reconstructs the residual approximately from a short history of random seeds and scalar rewards. Experiments on the Countdown arithmetic reasoning task with quantized Qwen2.5 models (1.5B and 3B) compare QES to a quantized zeroth-order baseline (QuZO), a no-tuning baseline, and a full-residual “oracle” variant, showing improved accuracy and training stability, especially for INT4.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The stagnation issue is clearly motivated: rounding small updates in an integer lattice can yield zero updates. The accumulated error feedback mechanism (Eqs. 6–8) is standard in spirit but appropriately adapted to discrete ES updates; the “temporal equivalence” argument via virtual parameters \(\Theta_t=W_t+e_t\) is a clear explanation of why residual accumulation prevents vanishing updates and bounds deviation by half a grid step (under the given rounding model). The seed-replay idea is plausible and is analyzed empirically via boundary-hit statistics.
- Weaknesses: Several key assumptions are not fully justified. (i) The seed replay rematerialization reuses current weights \(W_t\) for gating rather than historical \(W_\tau\); the paper argues sparsity makes \(W_\tau\approx W_t\), but this is only supported indirectly (Table 3) and lacks a direct measurement of replay-induced divergence (e.g., residual reconstruction error norm, or matching trajectories). (ii) The ES gradient estimator uses discrete perturbations \(\delta\) (Eq. 3) and then aggregates \(F_i\delta_i\) (Eq. 5); the estimator’s scaling, normalization of fitness, and the role of \(\sigma\) under discretization are not rigorously specified, making it hard to assess whether the estimator is unbiased/low-variance in the exact implemented setting. (iii) The claimed memory reduction “to inference level” is not quantified in experiments (no VRAM measurements), and stateless replay increases compute; wall-clock/throughput impact is not reported.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The method is explained with algorithms and intuitive motivation; the stagnation vs. residual accumulation story is easy to follow. Figures/tables support the main claims (training curves, ablations on \(K\) and \(\gamma\)).
- Weaknesses: Some definitions are informal or ambiguous (e.g., “fitness is normalized reward” but the exact normalization is omitted; the RLVR evaluation protocol is referenced but not concretely described). There are several typos/wording issues (e.g., “PQT,” “tur(en),” “limitated,” “makre”) that slightly distract.

Significance:
- Strengths: If the memory claims hold in practice, enabling full-parameter fine-tuning directly on INT4/INT8 weights without storing optimizer states would be impactful for low-resource adaptation and could broaden who can do post-quantization tuning.
- Weaknesses: The empirical validation is narrow: a single task (Countdown) and a single model family (Qwen2.5) with modest absolute accuracies. It is unclear how general the gains are for other reasoning, instruction-tuning, or alignment settings, and whether the method scales to longer-horizon RL-style optimization beyond this benchmark.

Originality:
- Strengths: Combining ES-based fine-tuning in quantized integer space with explicit residual-accumulation framing (delta-sigma / error feedback) and introducing a seed-replay mechanism for residual rematerialization is a novel packaging and appears non-trivial in this specific context.
- Weaknesses: Residual/error-feedback ideas are well-known in quantized/communication-efficient optimization; the main novelty is the adaptation to backprop-free ES and the specific “stateless” rematerialization approximation. The paper could more clearly delineate what is fundamentally new vs. adapted.

Overall, the paper has a strong and plausible core idea with promising results, but the evaluation and system-level claims (memory/compute tradeoff, generality) are not fully substantiated yet.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Reproducibility/specification: What is the exact fitness/reward normalization used in Eq. (2)/(5) and in Algorithm 1 (step 9)? Please provide the precise formula, including any baselining, ranking, whitening, or clipping.
2) Memory claim: Can you report actual GPU memory usage (peak VRAM) for (a) QuZO, (b) QES with seed replay, and (c) full-residual QES for each quantization setting? What parts dominate memory in QES (history buffer, RNG states, model copies, KV cache, etc.)?
3) Compute/throughput: What is the wall-clock overhead of stateless seed replay versus storing full residuals (oracle) and versus QuZO? Please report tokens/sec (or steps/sec) and total training time for the 300 generations.
4) Seed replay fidelity: Do the seed-replay and full-residual variants produce similar parameter trajectories? Please quantify reconstruction error (e.g., \(\|\tilde e_t - e_t\|\), mismatch rate in gating decisions, or final weight difference) rather than only boundary-hit ratios.
5) Generality: Do the gains persist on additional tasks or settings (e.g., another arithmetic/logic benchmark, different prompt templates, or different model families)? Even a small additional benchmark would affect confidence in significance.
review.limitations: The paper includes an Impact Statement but does not adequately discuss limitations. Suggestions: (i) explicitly state that evaluation is limited to Countdown and Qwen2.5 models and may not generalize; (ii) quantify and discuss the compute overhead of seed replay and potential energy costs; (iii) discuss failure modes (e.g., higher boundary-hit rates, instability when update sparsity assumptions break, sensitivity to \(\sigma,\alpha,\gamma,K\)); (iv) discuss potential misuse: enabling easier on-device fine-tuning could facilitate personalized malicious behavior or circumvention of safety measures.

title: Block removal for large language models through constrained binary optimization

review.summary: The paper proposes a method for pruning whole transformer blocks from large language models by casting block removal as a constrained binary optimization (CBO) problem. The authors introduce per-block gating variables that scale each block’s attention and FFN outputs, then use a second-order Taylor approximation of the loss with respect to these gates. Approximating the Hessian via outer products of per-sample gradients yields a quadratic objective over binary “remove/keep” variables with a cardinality constraint (remove exactly M blocks), which can be solved exactly for moderate depths or approximately via QUBO/Ising solvers. The paper emphasizes that not only the minimum-energy configuration but also low-energy excited states provide diverse, high-performing pruning patterns. Experiments on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (32 blocks) and Qwen3-14B (40 blocks), with short distillation-based retraining, show improved benchmark performance versus several block-removal baselines, especially on MMLU at high removal rates. A further case study on a heterogeneous hybrid/MoE model (NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-FP8) demonstrates removing a small number of MoE blocks without retraining while largely retaining GPQA and AIME25 accuracy for selected low-energy configurations.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The formulation is clear: introduce block gates, perform a second-order Taylor expansion, drop the linear term under a “near-stationary” assumption, and obtain a quadratic binary program with a fixed-number-of-blocks constraint. The Hessian approximation H≈(1/m)A^T A is standard in the sense that it is computable from per-sample gradients, and it yields a PSD quadratic objective, which is convenient for optimization/ranking. The paper also correctly highlights that the Hessian is computed once and reused for multiple M.
- Weaknesses: Several approximations are substantial but not empirically validated in the paper. In particular (i) the assumption ∇L(α0)≈0 for a “well-trained model” is asserted rather than checked, and the authors note prior work suggesting the linear term can help, yet no ablation is provided here. (ii) The Hessian approximation via A^T A is introduced without discussion of what gradients A contains exactly (per-token? per-sequence? averaged over positions?) and how that choice affects results. (iii) The mapping from “low quadratic energy” to “high downstream accuracy” is central but only indirectly supported (via some examples of excited states performing well); there is no quantitative correlation analysis between objective value and benchmark performance, which would strengthen the claim that energies are a strong proxy.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The method is described succinctly with equations and an implementation sketch; experiments are organized around (a) inspecting low-energy states and (b) comparing to baselines. Tables list removed block indices for reproducibility of configurations.
- Weaknesses: Key experimental details needed for reproducibility and interpretability are missing or deferred to code that is not included in the submission: exact distillation loss, optimizer/schedule, learning rate, sequence length, number of steps, and how logits/targets are formed. The description of the Hessian construction is underspecified (what constitutes a “sample,” how gradients are accumulated, whether mixed precision is used, etc.). The Nemotron experiment uses “AIME25” and NeMo Skills evaluation but does not describe the prompting/evaluation protocol beyond naming the library. Some baseline descriptions are also thin (e.g., “norm ratio” is used as a baseline but the metric/implementation is not described in-paper).

Significance:
- Strengths: Block removal is practically relevant because it reduces depth and inference cost without requiring specialized kernels. Explicitly modeling block interactions (quadratic terms) addresses a real weakness of greedy/heuristic depth pruning. The “excited states can be better than the ground state” observation is potentially useful in practice as it encourages exploring multiple near-optimal configurations.
- Weaknesses: The demonstrated improvements are concentrated on a subset of benchmarks (notably MMLU), while for others the gains are small or mixed; in some settings SWM performs better on GSM8K in the table. The method’s practicality at larger depths/removal counts is argued but not demonstrated: the paper suggests approximate solvers will work because many low-energy states are good, but provides no results using approximate solvers or on models with substantially more blocks.

Originality:
- Strengths: Applying a combinatorial second-order objective to *block-level* removal and emphasizing the use of the low-energy spectrum (not only the optimum) provides a distinct angle compared to typical block importance heuristics and iterative greedy pruning. The fixed-cardinality constrained formulation (and reuse across M) is clean.
- Weaknesses: The core technical ingredients (second-order Taylor pruning, Gauss-Newton-like/outer-product Hessian approximation, QUBO/Ising mapping) are incremental in isolation; the novelty mainly lies in the specific application to block gating and the empirical finding about excited states. Stronger novelty claims would benefit from deeper analysis of why interactions matter and when excited states outperform.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How exactly is the gradient matrix A in Eq. (6) constructed for the Hessian approximation (per token vs per sequence; averaged across positions; microbatching; any damping/regularization)? Please provide a precise algorithm.
2) What is the empirical correlation between the CBO objective value (energy) and downstream benchmark performance across many sampled/pruned configurations (not just a few low-energy states)? A scatter plot / Spearman correlation would directly support the “energy is a strong proxy” claim.
3) How sensitive are results to dropping the first-order term in Eq. (3)? Can you provide an ablation where the linear term is included (as in the cited prior work) and report whether it changes the selected blocks and benchmark outcomes?
4) The retraining uses knowledge distillation for one/half epoch. What are the exact distillation settings (loss form, temperature, mixing with ground-truth CE, LR schedule, max steps/tokens), and are conclusions robust to varying retraining budget (e.g., 0, small, larger)?
5) For Nemotron, you restrict removals to MoE layers. How would the method behave if all block types were allowed (Mamba/attention/MoE), and is the Hessian objective comparable across heterogeneous block types (i.e., does α attach identically and does scaling affect components similarly)?
review.limitations: Partially. The impact statement focuses on positive effects (efficiency, energy, access) but does not discuss key limitations/risks. Suggested additions: (i) the method relies on a second-order approximation around α=1 and may fail when pruning is severe or when gradients are not near-stationary; (ii) compute/memory costs of per-sample gradients for Hessian approximation and how this scales with calibration size and sequence length; (iii) potential distribution shift: calibration data choice may bias which blocks are removed and harm capabilities not represented; (iv) safety implications: compression may disproportionately degrade alignment/safety behaviors or increase hallucinations, and this should be evaluated explicitly.

title: Learning Sparse Visual Representations via Spatial-Semantic Factorization

review.summary: The paper proposes STELLAR, a self-supervised framework that replaces the standard dense n×d ViT feature grid with a sparse, factorized latent representation Z(X)=L(X)S(X), where S (r×d) contains r semantic “concept” tokens (“what”) and L (n×r) contains per-patch convex combination weights (“where”). This factorization is motivated as resolving an “invariance paradox”: semantic learning benefits from view-invariant features while reconstruction requires spatially equivariant features. STELLAR trains an encoder that outputs S and constructs L via cosine-similarity softmax between dense patch features and sparse tokens; a lightweight decoder reconstructs the image (via MaskGIT-VQGAN tokens) from Z. To induce semantic invariance and token consistency across augmentations despite the unordered token set, the method uses (i) online clustering of tokens into prototypes with Sinkhorn-balanced assignments and (ii) set-to-set token alignment across views using entropy-regularized optimal transport (Sinkhorn), plus optional CLS-token alignment and KoLeo regularization for token diversity. Experiments on ImageNet-1K show that with as few as 16 tokens, STELLAR achieves strong reconstruction quality and competitive semantics (linear probing), and improves dense-feature segmentation transfer on several benchmarks relative to many ImageNet-only SSL baselines; ablations study the role of reconstruction, clustering, and alignment losses, and the effect of different backbone priors (MAE/DINO/random).
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The factorized representation and the training objectives are clearly defined (reconstruction, clustering, OT-based set alignment, optional CLS alignment, KoLeo). The architecture for producing S (latent queries in ViT) and L (softmax over similarities between dense and sparse embeddings) is concrete and appears implementable. The paper includes targeted diagnostics supporting the key claim of “equivariant partitioning” (S stable, L changing under shifts) and ablations showing collapse or degradation when removing alignment/clustering.
- Weaknesses / concerns: (1) The “invariance paradox” argument is presented via differential constraints and an inequality involving σ_max(∂D/∂Z), but the derivation is informal and not rigorous; as stated, it reads more as intuition than a theorem. (2) Reconstruction evaluation relies on FID computed from reconstructions of VQGAN tokens (decoder predicts discrete tokens). The paper does not fully specify how FID is computed in this setting (e.g., whether images are decoded back to RGB by a fixed VQGAN, and whether the same VQGAN is used across methods), and whether the baselines’ decoders are comparable; TiTok is noted to use a much larger decoder, while for other baselines reconstruction is performed by training “the same decoder in STELLAR on top of frozen features,” which is a nonstandard and potentially confounding comparison. (3) The OT matching uses argmax over a soft transport plan; sensitivity to ε, number of Sinkhorn iterations, and failure modes (e.g., many-to-one matches) are not deeply characterized in the main text.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well-structured with a clear motivation (“what/where”), explicit formulas, and informative figures/tables (factorization schematic, robustness diagnostics, main reconstruction/semantics table, transfer benchmarks, and ablations).
- Weaknesses: Some critical experimental details that affect interpretation are relegated to the appendix or unclear: exact reconstruction target and pipeline for baselines; whether reconstructions are from identical latent dimensionalities; and which representation is used for each downstream metric (sparse vs dense vs CLS) sometimes varies and can confuse readers despite Table 5.

Significance:
- Strengths: If the reported trade-off improvements hold, learning a compact set of tokens that supports both high-quality reconstruction and strong semantics is valuable for efficient vision backbones and potentially for multimodal interfaces. The method also appears to improve dense-feature transfer for segmentation while learning primarily through sparse-token objectives.
- Weaknesses: The strongest headline numbers rely on ViT-H and substantial compute (multi-A100 training), and the semantic gains over strong ImageNet-only JE baselines are mixed (e.g., DINO CLS remains stronger for ViT-B linear probing). The core practical significance therefore depends on whether the “both semantics and reconstruction” advantage remains under tighter compute/architecture constraints and under more standardized reconstruction comparisons.

Originality:
- Strengths: The particular combination of (i) explicit low-rank feature-map factorization into concept tokens and spatial mixture weights, (ii) reconstruction through low-rank reconstitution of a dense map, and (iii) OT-based set alignment of sparse tokens across views is a novel and coherent design aimed at disentangling invariance/equivariance.
- Weaknesses: Several components are adapted from established ideas (latent queries, Sinkhorn-balanced clustering, view alignment, KoLeo), so novelty is more in the overall integration and the specific factorized latent format than in individual techniques.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Reconstruction evaluation fairness: For Table 1, how exactly is FID computed for each method (including MAE/DINO dense tokens and STELLAR)? Are reconstructions decoded to RGB using the same fixed VQGAN for all, and are image resolutions and postprocessing identical? Please provide the precise pipeline and whether any method uses additional pretrained components.

2) Baseline reconstruction protocol: You state you “trained the same decoder in STELLAR on top of the frozen features from different encoders.” Does this mean baselines are evaluated with a decoder they were not trained with (except TiTok*)? If so, how should we interpret FID/LPIPS as properties of the representation rather than of the decoder capacity/mismatch? Do you have results using each baseline’s native generative head/training objective where applicable (e.g., MAE’s own decoder), or an argument for why your protocol is the right comparator?

3) OT alignment sensitivity and stability: How sensitive are results (collapse vs success, final accuracy/FID) to the OT entropy regularization ε, the number of Sinkhorn iterations, and the argmax extraction of σ(j′)? Have you observed failure modes (e.g., repeated matches) and how are they mitigated?

4) Spatial constraints on L: Equation (1) states constraints 0≤L≤1 and L1=1. In practice L is a softmax over similarities (Eq. 14), but do you use any additional regularization to encourage sparsity/peakedness or spatial contiguity? How does τ_spatial impact reconstruction/semantics trade-offs beyond what is shown?

5) Token-count trade-off: Fig. 2(c) suggests semantics decrease as r increases (while reconstruction improves). Can you explain mechanistically why increasing rank hurts linear probing on mean-pooled sparse tokens, and whether alternative pooling/aggregation (e.g., attention pooling) removes this degradation?
review.limitations: No. The “Impact Statement” claims no societal consequences that must be highlighted, but the paper does not substantively discuss limitations or potential negative impacts. At minimum, the authors should: (i) acknowledge compute requirements and dependence on large-scale training for best results; (ii) discuss potential misuse cases enabled by improved reconstruction (e.g., image synthesis/forgery pipelines) and privacy considerations when training on sensitive imagery; (iii) clarify failure modes such as token collapse, sensitivity to hyperparameters (Sinkhorn/OT/temperatures), and potential brittleness across domains; and (iv) discuss that improvements are shown primarily on ImageNet-1K pretraining and may not generalize to other data distributions without further validation.

title: History-Guided Iterative Visual Reasoning with Self-Correction

review.summary: The paper proposes H-GIVR, an inference-time framework for multimodal VQA that aims to improve reliability beyond standard self-consistency (multi-sample + vote). H-GIVR (1) prompts the model to first generate an explicit visual description of the image, (2) performs iterative answering where the list of previous answers is appended as context to encourage review/self-correction, (3) periodically triggers “image re-observation” (on even iterations) to regenerate visual descriptions, and (4) terminates when an answer repeats (two identical answers), returning that as the final output (with safeguards such as a max-iteration cap). The paper evaluates H-GIVR on five benchmarks (ScienceQA, A-OKVQA, OK-VQA, VQAv2, TextVQA) across three MLLMs (Llama3.2-vision:11b, Qwen2.5vl:7b, Gemma3:12b) and compares against prompting baselines (FS-CoT, Auto-CoT, Active Prompt, Self-Consistency), reporting large accuracy gains at ~2.6–4.0 model calls on average.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The framework is clearly specified (Algorithm 1) and is easy to implement. The study includes multiple datasets, multiple models, several prompting settings, baseline comparisons, and an ablation separating the “visual description” and “iterative reasoning” components.
- Weaknesses: The experimental results as presented raise major validity questions. Several reported numbers are implausibly large (e.g., jumping from ~40% to ~85% on multiple datasets/models) without enough methodological detail to rule out confounds (evaluation protocol, data leakage, answer formatting constraints, few-shot content, etc.). For open-ended datasets (OK-VQA, VQAv2, TextVQA), the paper states it uses “accuracy” following prior work, but does not define the exact matching/scoring procedure; for these datasets, scoring details are crucial and can drastically change outcomes. Additionally, the stopping rule “first repeated answer” can be brittle: repetition does not necessarily imply correctness, and the paper does not analyze failure modes where the model repeats an early wrong answer. The “False” setting in Table 1 (injecting incorrect answers) is methodologically confusing and suggests the system may be benefiting from an unnatural oracle-like intervention or from prompt artifacts; the paper itself notes it is not practically deployable, but it is still used to motivate claims.

Presentation:
- Strengths: High-level idea is intuitive; figures and pseudocode help. The components (visual description, re-observation, historical-answer conditioning, confirmation mechanism) are understandable.
- Weaknesses: There are notable writing/formatting issues (e.g., the “!!!!” marker in Section 3.4), and some claims are contradictory or unclear (e.g., the text says H-GIVR with extra prompts has lower accuracy than without prompts, which is counterintuitive and not well explained). The description of prompts used for “Standard/Simple CoT/Complex CoT” is insufficiently concrete to reproduce. The paper does not specify sampling settings (temperature, top-p), maximum tokens, or how ties/normalization are handled for answer equality.

Significance:
- Strengths: If results are correct, a lightweight inference-time procedure that substantially boosts VQA across models/datasets with ~3 calls per question would be practically impactful.
- Weaknesses: Given the lack of scoring/protocol detail and the unusually large gains, the significance is hard to credit at face value. Also, the method is largely a prompting/interaction heuristic; it is not clear how robust it is across different deployment constraints (latency, context length, different MLLMs) or how it compares to simpler alternatives (e.g., just re-asking with the visual description once, or fixed small-N self-consistency with stopping).

Originality:
- Strengths: The particular combination of (a) explicit visual description as an “anchor”, (b) periodic re-observation, and (c) iterative conditioning on prior answers with an early-stop repetition criterion is a coherent, somewhat novel recipe for multimodal self-correction.
- Weaknesses: The components are incremental variations on existing prompt-based reflection/self-consistency ideas, and the paper does not deeply position what is fundamentally new beyond this recipe, nor provide theoretical/empirical analysis isolating why repetition-based stopping and even-iteration re-observation are the right choices versus other schedules/criteria.

Overall, the idea is promising and the experimental scope is broad, but the current presentation and missing evaluation details make the evidence insufficiently reliable for ICML.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) How exactly is “accuracy” computed for OK-VQA, VQAv2, and TextVQA (normalization rules, soft matching/VQA consensus scoring vs exact match, handling of multiple ground-truth answers)? Please provide the precise evaluation script or protocol.
2) What are the exact decoding/sampling parameters for all methods (temperature, top-p/top-k, random seeds, max tokens), and are they matched across baselines (Self-Consistency, Auto-CoT, etc.)? How sensitive are results to these choices?
3) How is “answer equality” determined for the Answer Confirmation Mechanism (case/whitespace/punctuation normalization, option-letter vs option-text for multiple choice, synonyms for open-ended)? Could premature stopping due to superficial string matches explain gains or failures?
4) Can you provide a breakdown of how often H-GIVR stops after 2, 3, 4, … iterations and the corresponding conditional accuracy (i.e., accuracy vs stopping time), plus an analysis of cases where it repeats an incorrect answer?
5) In Table 2, why do Simple/Complex CoT sometimes reduce accuracy compared to Standard when combined with H-GIVR? What exact prompts/few-shot exemplars were used, and do they contain dataset-specific artifacts?
review.limitations: No. While an Impact Statement is included, it is overly optimistic (“no foreseeable negative ethical consequences”) and does not discuss realistic risks: iterative self-correction can increase user over-trust, may still converge to consistent but wrong answers, and repeated calls increase exposure of sensitive images/questions to model providers (if not local). The paper should also discuss limitations around (i) brittleness of the repetition-based stopping rule, (ii) evaluation dependence on answer normalization/scoring, (iii) potential increases in latency/cost and carbon when scaled, and (iv) possible prompt-injection or adversarial examples where historical answers bias the model toward incorrect convergence.

title: Make Anything Match Your Target: Universal Adversarial Perturbations against Closed-Source MLLMs via Multi-Crop Routed Meta Optimization

review.summary:
The paper studies a black-box transfer setting for *universal targeted* attacks on closed-source multimodal LLMs (UniTTAA/UTTAA): for a given target image, learn a single additive perturbation (shared across inputs) that, when applied to arbitrary source images, makes commercial MLLMs produce outputs semantically matching the target.

To address instability and poor transfer when extending prior sample-wise feature-alignment attacks to this universal regime, the paper proposes a two-stage method (TarVRoM/MCRMO-Attack): (1) stabilize supervision by aggregating multiple randomly sampled target crops (Target-View / Multi-Crop Aggregation) plus an attention-focused crop as an anchor; (2) improve token-level alignment using an alignability-gated “token routing” mechanism that downweights non-alignable source tokens and performs a weighted optimal transport alignment to target prototypes; and (3) learn a meta-initialized perturbation prior across many target images (Reptile-style) so that per-target adaptation from few source images converges faster and yields better universal perturbations.

Experiments on 100 MSCOCO target images with N=20 optimization sources per target and 30 held-out sources for evaluation report gains in LLM-judge similarity/ASR and keyword matching when transferring to GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0, and Claude, including ablations on each component, number of target views, and effect of meta-initialization under varying adaptation budgets.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness (good):
- The paper clearly formulates universal targeted transfer (Def. III.1) and the surrogate empirical objective (Prop. III.2), then motivates why the universal setting increases gradient variance via “triple randomization.”
- The Target-View Aggregation argument (Prop. IV.1) is sound as a generic Monte Carlo variance reduction statement; it plausibly supports the design choice of averaging over multiple target crops.
- Token Routing is reasonably specified (prototype extraction via k-means; alignability via max cosine; sigmoid gating; Sinkhorn OT objective). The final objective combines global cosine alignment and routed local alignment.

However, several soundness gaps remain:
- The optimization described in Alg. 1/2 appears to update δ inside a nested loop over (x, v) ∈ X × V+, effectively applying sequential sign steps per pair; it is unclear whether gradients are recomputed after each inner update and whether this corresponds to optimizing the stated aggregate loss over the batch/product set. Clarifying the exact gradient estimate is important because sign updates can be sensitive to ordering.
- The definition of several key implementation details that affect conclusions is deferred to an Appendix not provided (surrogate encoder choices, adaptive weights Wi, crop distributions p(v), attention map extraction procedure, k-means hyperparameters K, Sinkhorn iterations/regularization). Reproducibility and interpretability of contributions depend on these.
- The evaluation relies on “LLM-as-a-judge” and a similarity threshold (ASR: similarity > 0.3) with GPTScore, but the paper does not describe judge prompt design, consistency checks, variance, or calibration. Given the tight coupling between metric and claims, more methodological detail is needed in the main text.

Presentation (good):
- The paper is generally well-structured: problem definition, method components (TVA/AFV, TR, MI), algorithms, and empirical results/ablations.
- Figures/tables communicate the main improvements clearly.

Weaknesses:
- Terminology and naming vary (TarVRoM vs TARVROM, UniTTAA vs UTTAA), and some notational inconsistencies appear (e.g., x^i marginal defined as 1/K but should match number of source tokens N; Eq. (13) sets x^i length K while source tokens are indexed by n=1..N; this is confusing and could be a typo with implications for OT setup).
- Loss definitions are sometimes ambiguous: Lglobal is written as cosine(g_adv, g_tar) but it is minimized/maximized? Eq. (15) adds these terms; depending on sign conventions, the optimization direction may be unclear.

Significance (good):
- Universal *targeted* transfer to closed-source MLLMs is a practically relevant and more stringent setting than sample-wise transfer, and the reported gains on unseen inputs are large relative to the universal baseline.
- The meta-initialization result (50 vs 300 epochs) suggests meaningful reduction in compute for per-target adaptation.

Limits to significance:
- The threat model is restricted to image-space perturbations with a specific norm budget and relies on surrogate encoders; it is not shown whether gains hold under broader prompts/tasks beyond caption-style evaluation.
- Claude results are much lower overall; it is unclear if the method generalizes broadly across MLLMs or mainly those closer to the surrogate ensemble.

Originality (good):
- The combination of multi-crop target aggregation + attention-selected anchor crop, alignability-gated token routing with OT, and cross-target meta-initialization is a novel integration for this setting.
- Individually, the components are natural extensions (variance reduction via multi-view, attention-guided cropping, token filtering, Reptile initialization), but applying and validating them in the universal targeted transfer-to-MLLM setting appears to be the main novelty.

Overall, the paper presents a coherent method with strong empirical gains, but leaves several key details (metric methodology and core hyperparameters) underspecified and contains at least one potentially important notational/technical inconsistency in the OT marginal definition.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Token routing OT formulation: In Eq. (13), the source marginal x^i is defined with length K (1/K,…,1/K), but source tokens are indexed by n=1..N. Is this a typo (should be 1/N over N tokens), or are you transporting from prototypes to tokens? Please provide the exact dimensions and confirm the Sinkhorn marginals used.

2) Objective sign conventions: Are you minimizing or maximizing cosine similarities in Eqs. (8), (14), and (15)? As written, Lglobal and Lroute increase with similarity; yet the optimization in Eq. (20) uses + sign(∇δ L). Please clarify the precise loss (e.g., negative cosine) and update direction.

3) LLM-as-a-judge evaluation: What is the exact judge model/prompting used to compute GPTScore and keyword matching? Did you measure judge variance (e.g., multiple runs, temperature) and sensitivity to the ASR threshold 0.3? This strongly affects the reported absolute ASR gains.

4) Surrogate ensemble and adaptive weights Wi: Which encoders comprise F, how are Wi computed (especially since credited to [1]), and how sensitive are results to the choice/size of the surrogate ensemble?

5) Meta-initialization scope: In Stage-1, is δ0 trained on the same 100 targets used for evaluation, or on a disjoint set of targets? If overlapping, can you report results when meta-training targets are fully disjoint from evaluation targets (you mention this exists in Appendix) and summarize the delta in the main paper?
review.limitations: No. The provided text does not include a dedicated limitations / broader impact discussion. At minimum, the paper should (i) discuss dual-use and potential misuse (e.g., evasion, manipulation, safety-bypass risks) and any mitigations such as responsible disclosure; (ii) clarify that LLM-as-a-judge metrics can be brittle and may not reflect real-world harmfulness; (iii) state the threat model boundaries (digital-only, perturbation budget, need for query access / transfer assumptions) and how results may change under common input sanitizations or different tasks/prompts; and (iv) discuss possible defenses and whether the proposed attack might spur an arms race, plus any ethical safeguards for releasing code/perturbations.

title: Reliable one-bit quantization of bandlimited graph data via single-shot noise shaping

review.summary: The paper studies low-bit quantization of graph signals that are bandlimited in the graph Fourier basis.
