Do you have a matched-parameter/control experiment (e.g., adding a second standard local-attention shortcut with the same LoRA budget)?
5) The method’s main claim is mitigating attention sinks via bounded-confidence dynamics. Beyond “first-token attention score” plots, can you provide quantitative sink metrics (e.g., entropy/concentration of attention, fraction of mass on top tokens) and correlate them with task improvements?
review.limitations: Partially. The appendix includes a limitations section (theoretical scope; hyperparameter sensitivity; LLM integration as auxiliary rather than replacement) and an impact statement, but the societal impact discussion is quite generic. It would be helpful to (i) discuss failure modes where strict locality/top-k could harm tasks requiring long-range dependencies (especially outside the auxiliary-LLM setting), (ii) more explicitly address that improved efficiency may enable larger-scale deployment (with associated environmental/misuse considerations), and (iii) include clearer guidance on hyperparameter tuning costs and how this affects real-world usability.

title: MieDB-100k: A Comprehensive Dataset for Medical Image Editing

review.summary: This paper introduces MieDB-100k, a ~112k-triplet dataset for text-guided medical image editing spanning 10 imaging modalities and 69 edit targets. The authors frame medical editing under three “perspectives”: (i) Perception (mask-painting overlays for organ/lesion/holistic segmentation to probe medical understanding), (ii) Modification (semantic lesion addition/removal and related content edits), and (iii) Transformation (low-level/global medical image processing such as denoising, artifact removal, contrast/windowing, and modality transfer). They propose a construction pipeline combining rule-based synthesis (e.g., alpha-blended overlays for perception; curated paired before/after processing for transformation) and modality-specific “expert” inpainting models (fine-tuned per modality) to generate lesion→healthy counterfactuals for modification, plus rejection sampling (VLM- or nnUNet-based) and clinician-in-the-loop manual curation for a benchmark subset. The paper also defines evaluation protocols/metrics: Dice-based localization (including a thresholded “Perception Accuracy”), background-only PSNR/SSIM for perception, PSNR/SSIM for transformation, and rubric-based VLM scoring plus clinician preference ranking for modification. Benchmarking across several open- and closed-source multimodal editing models is reported; finetuning OmniGen2 on MieDB-100k (OmniGen2-MIE) yields large gains across all three perspectives, with ablations and small OOD tests included.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The dataset is clearly defined as (I,P,O) triplets and the three-perspective taxonomy is coherent. For Perception, the mask overlay synthesis is deterministic and the paper provides a mathematically specified “alpha de-blending” procedure to recover masks for objective Dice evaluation. For Modification, the four-stage pipeline (modality-specific inpainting → counterfactual generation → rejection sampling → triplet pairing) is well motivated, and the paper includes manual inspection statistics (e.g., benchmark curation and sampled training QA with >95% rated high quality). The experimental section includes comparisons to multiple baselines, an ablation by perspective, and multi-round generation (Pass@3) to address stochasticity.
- Weaknesses: Several key details needed to fully trust the clinical fidelity and reproducibility are missing or underspecified. (i) The “modality-specific expert models” are said to be built on FLUX.1-Fill-dev with “parameter-efficient finetuning,” but the actual training data composition per modality (healthy-only selection criteria), prompts, masks, hyperparameters, and postprocessing details (background restoration/edge blending algorithms) are not fully specified in the main text; without this, Modification data quality is hard to independently verify. (ii) The rejection sampling uses a VLM for some modalities and nnUNet for others; false negatives/positives could bias the dataset toward “easy-to-verify” cases, but there is no quantitative analysis of filter accuracy or its impact on distribution. (iii) The Modification benchmark evaluation relies heavily on a single proprietary judge model (GPT-5.2) and a rubric; while reasonable, the paper does not report agreement with human ratings (correlation, consistency, inter-rater reliability). (iv) For Transformation tasks, the sources are “public medical image process repositories,” but the exact provenance and whether paired images are perfectly aligned/registered is unclear; misalignment could inflate/deflate PSNR/SSIM and also affect training.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is well organized with a clear motivation, a concise taxonomy (Perception/Modification/Transformation), and informative pipeline figures (Fig. 3, Fig. 6). Tables summarize baseline results and ablations clearly, and the appendix provides additional evaluation details and failure cases.
- Weaknesses: Some terminology and claims are stronger than what is directly supported (e.g., attributing baseline performance to “lack of medical knowledge” based solely on mask-painting performance under a specific overlay protocol). The benchmark size is sometimes described as “~100k” while the dataset is 112,228 triplets; the distinction between train/benchmark splits and their sizes is provided later but could be clearer earlier. Also, “Prompt rephrasing” uses Qwen-Max but the effect on performance or leakage risk is not deeply analyzed.

Significance:
- Strengths: A large, multi-modality medical editing dataset that includes both “understanding-as-edit” (mask painting) and generation-oriented edits is potentially valuable for training/evaluating unified multimodal editors in medical imaging. The breadth (10 modalities, 69 targets) and the inclusion of perception tasks are meaningful differentiators from prior datasets cited by the authors.
- Weaknesses: The benchmark portion is only 3,485 samples (with 618 for Modification and 451 for Transformation per Fig. 6), which may limit the statistical power and coverage of rare/complex cases. Additionally, many Modification examples are generated via inpainting models trained by the authors; this may bias models toward the artifacts and priors of that generator, potentially limiting real-world validity.

Originality:
- Strengths: The explicit unification of medical image understanding and editing via a mask-overlay editing formulation, plus the combination of modality-specific inpainting to produce lesion→healthy counterfactuals at scale, is a reasonably novel dataset-construction angle within the scope of the paper. The alpha de-blending reconstruction for objective evaluation of colored overlays is also a nice practical detail.
- Weaknesses: The core ingredients (using segmentation labels to create supervision; using inpainting to synthesize counterfactuals; VLM-based judging) are individually established ideas; the novelty is primarily in their integration and scale/coverage rather than a fundamentally new modeling or evaluation paradigm.

Overall, the paper’s main value is the dataset and construction/evaluation pipeline, with compelling benchmark improvements after finetuning. The biggest concern is the degree to which Modification/Transformation data and evaluations faithfully represent clinically meaningful edits versus artifacts and biases from the synthetic generation and automated filtering/judging.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Modification data generation: What exactly is the training recipe for the modality-specific inpainting expert models (data selection criteria for “healthy” images, mask generation strategy, prompts/conditioning, fine-tuning method and hyperparameters), and can you provide an ablation showing how Modification benchmark quality changes without the background restoration/edge blending steps?
2) Rejection sampling validity: What are the measured error rates of the Qwen3-VL and nnUNet filters (e.g., on a manually annotated subset of generated “healthy” images), and how much data is removed per modality/target? Does the filtering disproportionately remove harder cases, changing the task distribution?
3) Benchmark evaluation reliability: How well does the GPT-5.2 rubric score correlate with clinician preference rankings on the 618 Modification benchmark samples (e.g., Spearman/Pearson correlation), and what is the inter-rater agreement among the 3 clinician evaluators?
4) Transformation pairs: For each transformation target, are the (I,O) pairs pixel-aligned/registered and intensity-normalized? If not, how do you ensure PSNR/SSIM comparisons are meaningful, and how do you avoid models being penalized for benign global intensity scaling?
5) Data licensing and release: Since MieDB-100k aggregates many public datasets and also produces synthetic derivatives, what are the concrete redistribution/licensing terms and any de-identification checks that ensure the released triplets comply with upstream dataset licenses and privacy constraints?
review.limitations: No. The “Impact Statement” effectively states that no societal consequences need highlighting, which is not adequate for a medical image editing dataset/model adaptation paper. The paper should explicitly discuss (i) risks of misuse (fabricating medical evidence, training tools that could be used to alter clinical scans), (ii) the danger of deploying edited outputs in clinical decision-making, (iii) potential demographic/site/device biases inherited from source datasets, (iv) privacy considerations and license constraints when aggregating and redistributing derived medical images, and (v) how synthetic counterfactuals might encode unrealistic pathology distributions or artifacts that could mislead downstream models. The limitations section should also more directly acknowledge that Modification ground truth is synthetic and may not reflect real longitudinal counterfactuals.

title: Tool-Genesis: A Task-Driven Tool Creation Benchmark for Self-Evolving Language Agent

review.summary:
The paper introduces Tool-Genesis, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for requirement-driven tool creation by language agents in MCP (Model Context Protocol) format. Unlike spec-first settings, agents must infer tool contracts from abstract natural-language requirements, generate machine-checkable schemas, and materialize executable MCP servers. The benchmark contains 86 executable MCP servers (508 tools) across 24 domains, with 2,150 tasks/trajectories and 9,441 unit tests, constructed via crawling/filtering, LLM-generated tasks and trajectories validated via sandbox execution, unit-test extraction plus LLM synthesis, and multi-pass manual inspection.

Methodologically, the paper formalizes tool creation into two phases—Tool Interface Prediction and Tool Materialization—and evaluates them with a four-layer metric suite: (L1) format compliance and server executability, (L2) Schema-F1 via bipartite matching over embedded interface strings, (L3) functional correctness via soft/hard unit tests (including boundary/negative tests), and (L4) downstream task utility using a fixed proxy solver agent with an oracle-normalized success rate relative to ground-truth tools. Experiments across many LLMs compare direct one-shot generation versus a Code-Agent loop with execution feedback, showing large performance gaps and highlighting that small early interface/logic errors cascade into downstream failures; they also provide an initial finetuning exploration showing training on Tool-Genesis improves both one-shot generation and repair effectiveness.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The paper clearly separates interface inference from implementation (including an “oracle materialization” vs “cascaded materialization” framing), and proposes a multi-level evaluation that aims to localize failures (compliance/execution vs schema fidelity vs unit-tested functionality vs downstream utility). The dataset construction pipeline includes several quality controls: executable validation in a sandbox, trajectory grounding via real tool feedback, unit test extraction plus augmentation, and manual review with reported inter-annotator agreement (Cohen’s κ=0.85).
- Weaknesses / concerns: (i) The Layer-4 oracle-normalized SR definition appears problematic. Eq. (15) defines SR_j = (1 - s_gt_j)/(1 - s_gen_j + ε), which increases when s_gt is low and/or when s_gen is high, and can be >1; it also behaves counterintuitively when ground-truth succeeds perfectly (s_gt≈1 gives SR≈0 regardless of s_gen). If the intention is “generated utility as a fraction of oracle utility,” the current formula does not match that interpretation and could invert conclusions. This is a central metric, so it materially affects soundness. (ii) Schema-F1 relies on embeddings over serialized name+args with a threshold τ, but τ is not specified in the main description; results may be sensitive to τ and embedding choice, and semantic equivalence vs superficial similarity is unclear. (iii) The paper uses multiple LLM-as-judge steps (task filtering, trajectory validation, downstream outcome judging). While common, it introduces potential bias and variance; the paper does not quantify judge agreement, robustness across judges, or failure modes.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The benchmark motivation is clear (moving beyond spec-first and black-box outcome evaluation). The formalization (two-stage generation) and four-level metric suite are easy to follow, and the dataset pipeline is well-structured with explicit filtering stages and examples in the appendix. Tables/Figures communicate key takeaways (e.g., large gap between Direct and Code-Agent).
- Weaknesses: There are noticeable inconsistencies/typos in the results discussion (e.g., in §5.2 the text cites numbers that do not match Table 2, such as “UThard from 0.129 to 0.726” for Gemini-3-Flash, whereas Table 2 shows UThard 0.037→0.255; also mentions “SRsoft” though the table reports SR). Figure 7 is marked as a placeholder. Such issues reduce trust in careful reporting and reproducibility.

Significance:
- Strengths: A benchmark that (a) forces contract inference from requirements, (b) evaluates executable tool materialization, and (c) provides fine-grained diagnostic signals with unit tests including negative/boundary cases, addresses an important gap for self-evolving agents. The inclusion of real MCP servers across diverse domains and an execution-grounded pipeline could make it practically useful.
- Weaknesses: The benchmark scale (86 servers) is moderate, and the downstream evaluation depends on a fixed proxy agent and an LLM judge; without additional evidence of robustness, it is unclear how stable the L4 conclusions are across different solvers/judges or over time.

Originality:
- Strengths: The paper’s core contribution is the unified “full-lifecycle” diagnostic protocol (L1–L4) coupled with a requirement-driven MCP setting and a dataset grounded in executable MCP servers. The emphasis on decoupling tool quality from tool use via oracle materialization and a fixed downstream solver is a coherent design goal.
- Weaknesses: Several components resemble existing patterns (tool benchmarks, unit-test-based verification, LLM-as-judge filtering), so the novelty hinges on the specific combination and the requirement-driven/no-spec constraint plus MCP execution grounding. The claimed “oracle-normalized” measure is conceptually interesting, but (as written) its formula needs correction/clarification to be a defensible novelty.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Layer-4 metric: Can you clarify/correct the definition of Oracle-Normalized SR in Eq. (15)? As written, SR_j = (1 - s_gt)/(1 - s_gen + ε) seems counterintuitive and can reward low oracle performance; what is the intended normalization and range, and how would Table 2 change under the intended metric?
2) Schema-F1: What threshold τ is used for counting a matched pair as correct in Schema-F1, and how sensitive are the reported Schema-F1 results (and downstream correlations) to τ and to the embedding model choice?
3) LLM-as-judge reliability: For task filtering, trajectory validation, and downstream outcome scoring, what judge model(s) are used, and do you have any estimates of variance (e.g., repeated judging) or agreement with human evaluation on a sample?
4) Reproducibility of execution: Since servers are crawled and “not mirrored,” how will you ensure that the 86 MCP servers remain executable/stable for future benchmarking (version pinning, containerization, cached snapshots, or release artifacts)?
5) Result inconsistencies: Several numbers in §5.2 do not match Table 2 (e.g., Gemini UThard, mentions of SRsoft). Which source is authoritative, and can you provide an errata/updated table and text alignment?
review.limitations: No. The paper includes an ICML impact-statement placeholder rather than a concrete discussion. Given the benchmark’s use of crawled tool servers and code-generation/execution, the limitations section should (i) discuss safety risks of generating and executing code/tools (even in sandbox), (ii) potential dataset bias from the crawling/filtering process (domain coverage skew, exclusion of credentialed tools), (iii) brittleness over time as external servers change/disappear, and (iv) risks of enabling malicious tool creation or misuse and mitigation strategies (sandbox constraints, tool allowlists, responsible release).

title: DARC: Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding

review.summary: This paper studies inference-time alignment when human preferences are heterogeneous and annotators systematically disagree. It proposes DARC, a retraining-free decoding-time reranking method that, given a fixed candidate pool per prompt and multiple satisfaction samples (human multi-rater scores or proxy samples), selects responses using a risk-sensitive objective rather than mean reward alone. The core criterion is an entropic (KL-robust) value of satisfaction, with optional deployment controls via an entropic risk premium: (i) maximize entropic value; (ii) constrain the risk premium by a budget (τ); or (iii) penalize the risk premium (λ). The paper provides (a) a finite-sample lower-confidence-bound (LCB) justification that motivates a mean–dispersion surrogate, and (b) distributionally robust optimization (DRO) characterizations: KL-DRO yields the entropic objective, and χ²-DRO yields a mean–dispersion form. Empirically, DARC is evaluated on MT-Bench and AlpacaEval 2.0 using fixed candidate pools and both proxy-based evaluation and human-loop multi-annotator ratings, and it reports improvements in disagreement-related metrics, tradeoff scores, and prompt-level tail performance (CVaR) while maintaining comparable mean quality. The work also includes a multi-scorer extension that aggregates across multiple reward models via a soft worst-case (KL-regularized) operator to hedge scorer shift and proxy over-optimization.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The formulation is clear: conditional on a fixed candidate set, each candidate induces a satisfaction random variable over raters/users. The paper provides two complementary theoretical perspectives. (1) A uniform LCB (via empirical Bernstein + union bound) motivates penalizing disagreement/variance as an estimation-risk control; assumptions (bounded rewards / sub-Gaussian alternative) are stated and proofs are supplied in appendices. (2) The entropic objective is correctly linked to KL-regularized DRO via the Donsker–Varadhan variational formula, and the χ²-DRO bound produces a mean–dispersion form that aligns with the LCB penalty. The inference-time rules are precisely specified, including constrained/penalized forms and an ε near-tie rule.
- Weaknesses: The main algorithm relies heavily on proxy-based “disagreement” estimated as reward-model sensitivity under style-preserving perturbations. While the paper validates correlation with human disagreement, the theoretical LCB guarantees are for i.i.d. scalar satisfaction samples per candidate; the proxy setting is only covered via a uniform closeness assumption (Appendix A.12), which is not empirically calibrated into an actual bound. Thus, the strongest formal guarantees do not directly apply to the primary scalable deployment scenario. Additionally, the entropic objective is defined over the latent satisfaction distribution across users/raters; in practice it is computed from a small proxy sample set (perturbations, dropout, or multiple RMs), raising questions about whether the induced distribution corresponds to the intended preference heterogeneity.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is well-structured (setup → guarantees → method → experiments) and generally readable for an ICML audience. Definitions (entropic value, risk premium, constrained/penalized variants) are explicit. The appendices are extensive and include pseudocode, metric definitions, hyperparameters, and additional analyses (proxy validity, mismatch taxonomy, ablations). Reporting separates selection-time and evaluation-time raters in the human-loop setting to mitigate leakage.
- Weaknesses: There is some conceptual layering that may confuse readers: “risk” sometimes refers to estimation uncertainty (LCB), sometimes intrinsic preference heterogeneity, and sometimes reward-model sensitivity to perturbations. The paper does acknowledge these distinctions, but the experimental risk metric (perturbation sensitivity σ̂_sel) is not the same as the theoretical σ of human satisfaction and not the same as tail-risk measures; this can make it hard to interpret what type of robustness is being improved.

Significance:
- Strengths: Inference-time methods that do not require retraining are practically valuable, especially when alignment feedback is heterogeneous. The paper presents a coherent decision-theoretic framing and provides simple “deployment knobs” (β, τ/λ, ε) for risk budgeting. The empirical results show consistent improvements in tradeoff and tail metrics, with larger gains on high-disagreement prompts, and DARC appears complementary to robust training methods (cDPO/rDPO).
- Weaknesses: The demonstrated gains, while consistent, are mainly in composite metrics (Tradeoff = μ − λσ) and CVaR over prompts; the method’s impact depends on accepting the proxy disagreement measure as a meaningful operationalization. Also, the evaluations are limited to reranking within finite candidate pools; if candidate pools lack truly robust answers, decoding-time risk control may have limited upside.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of (i) disagreement-aware decoding framed as risk-constrained decision making, (ii) KL-robust entropic decoding with explicit risk-premium constraints/penalties, and (iii) a multi-scorer soft worst-case aggregation with a KL-regularized DRO interpretation, is a novel and fairly unified package in the context of inference-time alignment. The paper also clarifies how mean–dispersion heuristics can arise from LCB/DRO views.
- Weaknesses: Some components (entropic risk measures, DRO views, mean–variance/dispersion penalties, soft-min across scorers) are individually standard; the novelty is more in the alignment-specific instantiation and empirical demonstration than in introducing fundamentally new mathematical tools.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) In the proxy setting, what evidence supports that “style-preserving perturbation sensitivity” is a faithful proxy for *human* preference heterogeneity for the *same candidate* (s,y), rather than primarily measuring reward-model surface-form instability? Can you quantify how often DARC’s gains persist if σ̂ is computed from human ratings (where available) but selection still uses proxy μ̂?

2) How sensitive are the conclusions to the particular reward model used for scoring/perturbation sensitivity in the single-scorer experiments (Table 1/14)? The multi-scorer experiment evaluates improvements relative to base across scorers, but do the main single-scorer gains hold under a different primary RM for both selection and evaluation?

3) For DARC-τ, τ is set via a quantile rule over RPβ within each prompt’s candidate pool. How does this compare to using a *global* τ (shared across prompts) in terms of feasibility, stability, and the reward–risk trade-off? Would a global budget be more interpretable as a deployment control?

4) The human-loop evaluation uses disjoint selection and evaluation rater sets. What are the concrete values of n (per-candidate selection ratings) and K (pool size) in the human-loop setting, and how do results vary with n and K in the human setting (not just proxy ablations)?

5) When the proxy mismatch taxonomy shows many false positives driven by surface-form sensitivity, does DARC-ε ever systematically select shorter/more templated answers that “game” the RM stability proxy? Beyond average length, can you report any qualitative or metric-based checks for regressions in content richness/helpfulness due to stability-seeking behavior?
review.limitations: yes. The paper explicitly notes key limitations: dependence on finite candidate pools, scorer bias/shift, and that perturbation-based disagreement proxies are screening signals rather than calibrated estimates of human disagreement. The impact statement acknowledges potential bias encoded in proxies/scorers and recommends auditing and sensitivity reporting. A constructive addition would be to discuss potential failure modes where reducing disagreement could undesirably suppress minority/atypical but valuable responses, and to outline safeguards or evaluation protocols to ensure minority-preference protection (since “low disagreement” is not always ethically preferable).

title: A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities

review.summary: The paper proposes NeuroCognition, a benchmark suite intended to evaluate foundational “cognitive primitives” of LLMs via adaptations of three classic neuropsychological tests: Raven’s Advanced Progressive Matrices (RAPM) for abstract relational reasoning, Spatial Working Memory (SWM) for systematic search/maintenance of state, and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) for cognitive flexibility and rule switching. Each test is instantiated in multiple modalities (text, image, and sometimes image+text) and difficulty settings, with process-aware metrics (e.g., SWM penalizing illegal/repeated/no-box moves; WCST using a per-rule efficiency score plus PR/FMS error rates). The authors evaluate a set of proprietary and open multimodal models under zero-shot settings, run ablations on “reasoning vs. no reasoning” for RAPM, provide “pattern hints” for RAPM, and add note-taking assistance for SWM/WCST as a form of cognitive offloading. Finally, the paper adds an exploratory factor analysis over 10 standard benchmarks for 156 models (using Artificial Analysis data) suggesting a single dominant general capability factor, and correlates NeuroCognition scores with select external benchmarks meant to reflect related abilities (Long HotPotQA, ARC-AGI 2, LLM Task Interference) as well as an aggregate “11-benchmark average.”
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The benchmark tasks are clearly specified, include multiple modalities and difficulty variants, and propose metrics that attempt to capture process failures rather than only end accuracy (notably SWM’s error taxonomy and WCST’s PR/FMS). RAPM text generation is made “verifiable” via stored constraints and an automatic validator, which is a strong design choice for reproducibility. The paper reports multiple runs for stochastic tasks (SWM/WCST) and provides means/std.
- Weaknesses: Several central claims rely on small-N correlation analyses (often N=10 models; ARC-AGI 2 correlations are N=6), which makes inferential conclusions fragile. The RAPM ablation uses paired t-tests across models (effectively treating models as samples), but the experimental unit is ambiguous: if per-item results exist, statistics should likely be computed over items per model, not over models, or via hierarchical methods. RAPM is only run once per model (n=140/200 items), while reasoning budgets and “overthinking” interventions differ across models (e.g., disabling reasoning only for some models and only for some tests), introducing confounds. The human baselines are not consistently comparable (RAPM uses an average from prior work; SWM/WCST use claimed worst-case scores under assumptions).

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is well organized, defines tasks and metrics explicitly with equations, and includes detailed appendices with generation/validation algorithms, prompts, and full tables. Failure mode analysis is concrete (RAPM qualitative snippets; SWM error-type counts; WCST PR/FMS).
- Weaknesses: Some important methodological choices are not fully justified or may confuse readers, e.g., why certain reasoning modes are disabled only for particular models/tests, and how “thinking budgets” are enforced (the paper says budgets are “not enforced as a hard token limit” for SWM/WCST). The factor analysis section depends on external leaderboard normalization; the exact preprocessing and missing-data handling are not described in depth.

Significance:
- Strengths: A neuropsychology-grounded benchmark that is multimodal and process-aware could be useful for diagnosing gaps not visible in standard task-completion benchmarks, and the observed modality/difficulty degradations and “reasoning not always helpful” result are potentially valuable to the community. The verifiable RAPM-text-gen component is a practical contribution.
- Weaknesses: Empirical conclusions about “distinct cognitive abilities beyond general capability” are only partially supported: correlations show NeuroCognition average is strongly correlated with the general benchmark average (r=.86), while some subtests (e.g., RAPM Image MC) show different behavior, but the evidence base is limited by small model counts and uncertain statistical treatment. Also, the benchmark currently evaluates a relatively small set of models directly (10), which limits the breadth of claims about LLMs generally.

Originality:
- Strengths: The combination of (i) adapting three classic neuropsych tests into a unified suite, (ii) adding multimodal and difficulty-controlled variants, and (iii) emphasizing process-aware scoring and “cognitive offloading” interventions is a distinctive package. The RAPM text generation + constraint-based validation is a relatively novel benchmark engineering aspect.
- Weaknesses: The individual test adaptations are conceptually straightforward, and prior work has applied some neuropsych tests to LLMs; the novelty is more in the benchmark integration, metric design, and systematic evaluation than in new modeling ideas.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Statistical unit and testing: For RAPM reasoning-vs-no-reasoning and pattern-hint experiments, what exactly is the paired t-test performed over (models, items, or runs)? Can you report per-item paired comparisons within each model and then aggregate (or use a mixed-effects model) to support the claim that disabling reasoning improves Text MC?

2) Reproducibility of “reasoning mode”: Many results hinge on “default reasoning” vs “no reasoning,” but the paper uses a mix of API reasoning toggles and prompt instructions, and in some cases notes budgets are not enforced. How do you verify that the intended reasoning condition was actually applied consistently across providers/models?

3) Human baselines: SWM/WCST use a claimed “healthy human worst-case” of 1.0 (SWM) and 5/7 or 5/9 (WCST). Were any human participants run on your exact task implementations (especially text variants), or are these purely theoretical bounds? If theoretical, can you justify that the interaction constraints (multi-turn, feedback format, ambiguity variants) indeed allow a cognitively normal human to always achieve those bounds?

4) Correlation claims with external benchmarks: Given the very small N (often 10, and N=6 for ARC-AGI 2), how sensitive are the reported correlations to the inclusion/exclusion of individual models? Can you provide confidence intervals or robustness checks (e.g., leave-one-out) for key correlations like RAPM Image MC vs ARC-AGI 2 and NeuroCognition Avg vs 11-benchmark Avg?

5) Dataset leakage / contamination: RAPM image uses RAVEN and text RAPM is synthetic. What steps are taken to reduce the risk that models have seen RAVEN items or close variants during training, and how would that affect your interpretation of RAPM as measuring fluid reasoning?
review.limitations: yes. The paper includes a limitations section addressing sample size/cost, the validity of transferring human neuropsychological constructs to LLMs (psychometric validity/reliability/invariance), and the need for further validation across prompts and LLMs. The impact statement appropriately avoids claims about consciousness/self-awareness. One improvement would be to more explicitly discuss risks of over-interpreting “human deficits” from these tests (anthropomorphism) and to add a short discussion of potential misuse (e.g., using such scores as a proxy for human intelligence or for high-stakes model deployment decisions).

title: Conditionally Site-Independent Neural Evolution of Antibody Sequences

review.summary:
The paper proposes COSINE, a conditionally site-independent continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) model for antibody sequence evolution. COSINE uses a neural network (initialized from ESM2) to output per-site amino-acid substitution rate matrices conditioned on the full parent sequence, yielding a factorized transition likelihood over sites. The authors provide theory connecting this factorized CTMC to a full sequential point-mutation CTMC over the exponentially large sequence space: (i) a bound showing COSINE’s transition distribution is a first-order approximation to the true process with an L1 error scaling as O(t^2) in branch length, under a rate-matching assumption for single-step mutants; and (ii) a lemma that Gillespie sampling using COSINE’s instantaneous rates exactly samples from the true sequential point-mutation CTMC when the same single-step rate-matching condition holds along the sampled trajectory.

For fitness inference, the paper proposes a selection score defined as a log-likelihood ratio between COSINE’s transition likelihood and a pretrained somatic hypermutation (SHM) model (Thrifty), aiming to disentangle selection from mutation biases. For controlled generation/optimization, the paper introduces Guided Gillespie: a classifier-guided modification of Gillespie sampling where instantaneous rates are reweighted by an affinity predictor; to make this efficient it uses a first-order Taylor approximation so each step needs only one gradient evaluation.

Empirically, COSINE is trained on ~2M parent-child transitions extracted from ~120k clonal families across five public BCR sequencing sources. The paper reports improved held-out transition likelihood vs DASM+Thrifty, improved zero-shot variant effect prediction (Spearman correlation) on several FLAb2 DMS assays compared to multiple protein/antibody LMs and DASM, and demonstrates guided sampling that increases predicted neutralization scores against SARS-CoV targets while maintaining humanness and structural plausibility metrics. Supplementary synthetic experiments on a small codon state space validate the O(t^2) approximation behavior and the benefit of Gillespie sampling over the factorized matrix-exponential sampler under epistasis.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness (good):
- Clear formulation of the COSINE likelihood as a product over per-site matrix exponentials with rates conditioned on the full sequence (Eq. 2), which is computationally tractable.
- The theoretical result (Prop. 4.1 / D.1) is well-motivated and uses a standard uniformization argument to show that if single-mutation transition probabilities match (i.e., row-wise agreement on the immediate neighborhood), then differences arise only from paths with >=2 jumps, yielding an O((λt)^2) bound. The proof appears internally consistent.
- The Gillespie lemma (Lemma 4.2 / D.2) is also standard: matching holding times and jump probabilities implies identical CTMC.

Weaknesses for soundness:
- The key rate-matching assumption needed for both theoretical guarantees is strong and not actually enforced by the proposed MLE training objective (which optimizes a factorized finite-time likelihood). The authors acknowledge bias from marginalizing intermediate states on longer branches (Sec. 4, Sec. C.1), but the main paper’s narrative sometimes leans on guarantees that only hold “if COSINE recovers instantaneous rates.” In the real antibody setting, there is limited direct evidence that the learned rates satisfy the neighborhood matching condition.
- The SHM/selection disentanglement score (Eq. 5) relies on a small-t approximation (log p ≈ log Q + const) and then uses a fixed t=0.2 for all DMS assays. It is plausible but not fully justified that this fixed-t choice is optimal/robust across datasets and mutational distances (especially for multi-aa mutant datasets like Shanehsazzadeh where avg substitutions ~5–6).
- Guided Gillespie optimizes predicted affinity using external predictors and demonstrates that large guidance strengths can “exploit oracle uncertainty” (Sec. 5.4). This is a known failure mode, but here it directly affects the main optimization claim; the evaluation is entirely in-silico.

Presentation (good):
- The paper is generally well-structured: background on CTMCs, independent-sites models, sequential point-mutation processes; then COSINE definition, theory, and applications.
- Key algorithms (Gillespie and Guided Gillespie) are provided with pseudocode, and the supplement contains additional validations.

Weaknesses for presentation:
- Some experimental claims depend on appendix-only details (e.g., perplexity definition, exact preprocessing, and various ablations). While acceptable, it makes it harder to assess reproducibility and to understand what aspects are crucial.
- The relationship between “factorized sampling via Eq. (2)” vs “Gillespie sampling using COSINE rates” could be emphasized earlier: the model is trained with the factorized finite-time likelihood, but recommended sampling uses Gillespie to better approximate a sequential point-mutation process. This distinction is important for readers and for interpreting theory.

Significance (good):
- Modeling antibody affinity maturation as a neural-parameterized CTMC that conditions on full sequence context is a meaningful attempt to combine phylogenetic process modeling with deep sequence modeling.
- The selection-score approach using an SHM likelihood ratio is practically relevant for antibody VEP, and the reported improvements over multiple baselines on FLAb2 assays are substantial.

Weaknesses for significance:
- The downstream “optimization” demonstrations rely on predicted binders/humanness/structure proxies rather than experimental validation, limiting the strength of the design claims.
- The VEP evaluation is on a relatively small set of DMS assays (4 sources, 7 splits in Table 1). While the results are strong, it is unclear how broadly they generalize.

Originality (good):
- The core modeling choice—site-independent transitions conditioned on the entire sequence context via per-site rate matrices—sits between independent-sites phylogenetics and expressive deep sequence models in a clean way.
- The explicit approximation connection to sequential point-mutation CTMCs, plus the use of Gillespie sampling with learned rates and classifier-guided rate reweighting (with a Taylor approximation for efficiency), constitutes a reasonably novel combination within the paper’s scope.

Overall, the paper is technically interesting with strong empirical results on the chosen benchmarks, but some central guarantees hinge on assumptions not demonstrated to hold in the large-scale antibody setting, and the optimization results remain in-silico and predictor-dependent.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Rate-matching / instantaneous-rate validity: Do you have quantitative evidence on real antibody data that the learned instantaneous neighborhood rates (Qθ(x)ℓ)xℓ,a correlate with (or are calibrated to) true single-step mutation propensities, beyond improved finite-time likelihood? For example, can you evaluate one-step mutation prediction (t→0 regime) or compare implied single-step jump probabilities against any held-out short-branch subset?

2) Choice and sensitivity of t in VEP: You fix t=0.2 for all DMS scoring. How sensitive are the reported Spearman correlations to this choice per assay, especially for multi-mutant datasets (Shaneh. avg ~5–6 substitutions) and for the Adams dataset (avg ~2)? Would selecting t via validation on each assay change conclusions vs baselines?

3) Selection-score disentanglement: Since q(y|x,t) (Thrifty) is computed in codon space and then marginalized to amino acids, while pθ(y|x,t) is amino-acid CTMC, does the mismatch in state spaces introduce systematic bias (e.g., favoring amino acids with many codons)? Have you tried alternative normalizations or controls to verify Eq. (5) is not partially driven by codon-degeneracy artifacts?

4) Guided Gillespie evaluation: The guidance experiments use heavy-chain-only predictors, but COSINE conditions on paired sequences (sometimes). How is the light chain handled during guided sampling (kept fixed, absent, or included with a separator)? If absent/fixed, how does this affect claims about modeling inter-chain epistasis for design?

5) Baseline comparability and training compute: COSINE is initialized from ESM2-150M and trained end-to-end on ~2M transitions. Are any baselines fine-tuned on the same clonal transition dataset, or are they purely pretrained models? A compute/finetuning comparison would clarify whether gains come from the evolutionary objective vs simply from supervised adaptation to this dataset.
review.limitations: Partially. The paper discusses two methodological limitations (first-order approximation/model misspecification and ignoring indels) and includes an impact statement. However, the limitations section could more directly address: (i) dependence on phylogenetic reconstruction/ancestral reconstruction and associated errors (tree inference with IQ-TREE + ASR), (ii) reliance on external SHM model quality for selection-score validity, and (iii) risks/limitations of classifier-guided optimization with imperfect or exploitable predictors (they mention oracle uncertainty exploitation, but could discuss mitigation and broader misuse risks in antibody design).

title: GFlowPO: Generative Flow Network as a Language Model Prompt Optimizer

review.summary: The paper proposes GFLOWPO, a two-step framework for automatic discrete prompt optimization for language models. It frames prompt search as posterior inference over prompts z given a small task dataset D and a meta-prompt M, using a reference language model as a conditional prior pref(z|M). In STEP-A, a “prompt-LM” is fine-tuned to approximate the (unnormalized) posterior via an off-policy GFlowNet-style objective (using a PCL/TB-like squared consistency loss with VarGrad minibatch estimation of the log-partition), with a replay buffer that reuses past prompt evaluations to improve sample efficiency. The reward is defined as training accuracy (correct count) times the reference-LM prior probability pref(z|M). In STEP-B, the method updates the meta-prompt using a training-free Dynamic Memory Update (DMU): it injects a small set of reference prompts sampled both from a replay buffer (for diversity/exploration) and a high-reward buffer (for exploitation), aiming to improve a marginal-likelihood / variational-bound motivation. The approach is evaluated on few-shot text classification (GLUE/SuperGLUE subsets), instruction induction (II and BBII) for both classification and exact-match generation tasks, and multiple-choice QA (MMLU and OpenBookQA), across various prompt-LM/target-LM pairs, showing improvements over several baselines including StablePrompt.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The paper clearly defines the optimization target and provides a coherent probabilistic framing (posterior inference with a reference-LM prior) that motivates both (i) sampling proportional to reward (GFlowNet objective) and (ii) adapting the meta-prompt to concentrate search. The off-policy replay mixture policy is well specified (Eq. 7) and the algorithm is given (Algorithm 1). The reward construction R(z;M)=A_D(z)·pref(z|M) is operational and the need to recompute the prior under changing M is acknowledged.
- Weaknesses: Several key steps are heuristic/under-justified relative to the claimed inference objective. First, the method replaces p(D|z) with training accuracy A_D(z), departing from the Bayesian framing; while Appendix A motivates correlation with test accuracy, this is still a mismatch between Eq. (2)/(3)/(8) and the implemented reward (Eq. 4). Second, the DMU update is motivated via a variational lower bound (Eq. 8) but the actual update (sampling a few prompts from B and Q into Z_ref) is not shown to optimize that bound even approximately; the argument about reducing KL by “blending” is intuitive but not formal, and it is unclear how sensitive performance is to this specific template-based injection. Third, the GFlowNet objective is presented as a global squared error between log p_θ and log R with a batch-estimated logZ; the paper does not provide analysis of convergence/stability under the non-stationary reward induced by updating M (STEP-B) and updating the replay distribution, beyond EMA smoothing. Overall, the approach is plausible and empirically validated, but the theoretical connection to posterior inference is looser than suggested.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well organized: it introduces the two-step method, gives equations, provides a concrete meta-prompt template, and includes pseudocode. Experimental sections are structured by task type, and ablations isolate off-policy vs DMU contributions.
- Weaknesses: Some notation and naming is slightly confusing/inconsistent (GFLOWPO vs GFlowPO in several places). The description of the “reference LM” pref as a deepcopy of p_θ at initialization is important but could be emphasized earlier, since it affects the interpretation of pref as a fixed prior. Also, the evaluation protocol relies on selecting best prompt from a high-reward buffer; this is reasonable but could be stated more prominently as it influences comparisons.

Significance:
- Strengths: Prompt optimization remains practically important, and the paper targets a concrete pain point: sample efficiency under expensive target-LM calls. The combination of off-policy replay training and meta-prompt adaptation is practically relevant. The method is evaluated across multiple task families (classification, induction/generation, QA) and multiple model pairings, suggesting some breadth.
- Weaknesses: The reported gains are sometimes modest on key benchmarks (e.g., MMLU: 55.6 vs StablePrompt 55.8), and some BBII classification tasks show regressions relative to StablePrompt (Table 11). The work’s main value is as a better engineering of prompt search rather than a clearly new capability; impact may depend on whether the sample-efficiency improvements translate to substantially fewer target-LM queries, which is not directly quantified.

Originality:
- Strengths: Using an off-policy GFlowNet-style objective for discrete prompt optimization, combined with a training-free, memory-based meta-prompt update that injects both diverse and top prompts, is a novel combination within the prompt optimization setting presented. Framing prompt search as posterior inference with a reference-LM prior is also a useful unifying perspective.
- Weaknesses: Core components (replay/off-policy RL, prompt memory injection, selecting top prompts) are individually conceptually close to existing ideas; the novelty is primarily in assembling them under the GFlowNet formalism and the specific DMU mechanism.

Empirical evaluation (cross-cutting):
- Strengths: Comparisons include a strong direct baseline (StablePrompt) and multiple other prompt optimization methods. Results are reported with mean/std for GFLOWPO, and ablations (Table 4, Table 5) support the role of DMU and pre-step.
- Weaknesses: It is not fully clear that compute/query budgets are matched against all baselines (many baseline numbers are “taken from” StablePrompt prior work), and GFLOWPO’s key claim is sample efficiency yet the paper largely reports final accuracy rather than accuracy vs number of target-LM evaluations across tasks (only one analysis plot on II tasks). Additionally, several tasks use exact match, but the paper does not discuss sensitivity to decoding settings (greedy vs sampling) or to prompt length constraints beyond a max length hyperparameter.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Budget matching / sample efficiency: For the main comparisons (Tables 1–3), are the numbers for StablePrompt/APE/ProTeGi obtained under the same target-LM query budget (number of evaluated prompts × number of examples) as GFLOWPO? If not, can you provide accuracy vs #target-LM-evaluations curves (like Fig. 5) for the main benchmarks?
2) Reward/prior interaction: How sensitive is performance to the pref(z|M) factor in R(z;M)=A_D(z)·pref(z|M)? In particular, what happens if you drop pref (pure accuracy reward) or anneal its weight, and does DMU still help?
3) DMU mechanism: Can you clarify the exact formatting/injection of Z_ref into the meta-prompt and whether ordering matters? Have you tested alternative update rules (e.g., only top prompts, or diversity sampling by clustering) under the same budget, and how robust is DMU to kb/kq choices beyond kb=2,kq=1?
4) Non-stationarity and replay: Since M changes every iteration (Table 6: M-step frequency 1) and thus pref(z|M) changes, replay samples are evaluated under a moving reward. Did you observe instability from this non-stationarity, and did you try less frequent DMU updates or reward correction strategies?
5) Reproducibility details: Please specify decoding parameters for prompt generation (top-p, top-k, max new tokens, stop conditions) and for target-LM answering, since exact-match tasks can be sensitive to these choices.
review.limitations: Partially. The paper includes a short limitations section (lack of evaluation on reasoning-centric tasks; task-specific optimization; potential benefit from test-time compute) and an impact statement asserting no unique ethical concerns. However, it does not discuss several practical/risks limitations that seem relevant: (i) potential overfitting to small dev/train sets when selecting best-of-buffer prompts; (ii) computational and environmental costs of repeated target-LM querying (central to the motivation); (iii) possible misuse where automated prompt optimization could be used to optimize harmful prompts (jailbreaks), especially since the method improves exploration; and (iv) dependence on the reference-LM prior potentially encoding biases or constraining prompts in undesirable ways. I recommend adding a clearer discussion of these points and any mitigations (e.g., safety filters, evaluation on harmful prompt generation, or guidance on responsible use).

title: Efficient Analysis of the Distilled Neural Tangent Kernel

review.summary:
The paper studies how to make empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) computations tractable for modern networks by compressing both the dataset dimension and the parameter/gradient dimension. The authors formalize “data redundancy” via low truncation rank of per-class NTK Gram matrices and “parameter redundancy” via existence of a low-dimensional parameter subspace that approximately preserves the NTK.

A key conceptual contribution is an interpretation of dataset distillation (in a frozen/lazy regime) as selecting a tangent-feature subspace in parameter space: distilled inputs induce a subspace spanned by logit gradients, and a one-step smoothness/regret analysis shows that outer-objective progress is governed by projection residual onto this subspace. The paper connects this subspace view to an inducing-point/Nyström form for the NTK.

Methodologically, the proposed Distilled NTK (DNTK) pipeline applies: (1) NTK-tuned dataset distillation (instantiated with WMDD) to reduce the number of inputs for which Jacobians are computed; (2) Johnson–Lindenstrauss (JL) random projection of gradients to reduce parameter dimension; and (3) a “local-global gradient distillation” procedure (Algorithm 1) that synthesizes a small set of representative gradients/labels using spectral clustering and local/global eigenmodes of an averaged class kernel. Experiments on ImageNette (and additional ImageWoof results) show that per-class kernels exhibit low effective rank and that Algorithm 1 can significantly outperform gradient sampling baselines at high compression, while maintaining predictive fidelity of kernel ridge regression approximations to a reference network.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Clear high-level goal and a coherent three-stage compression story: distill inputs (reduce Jacobian evaluations), project gradients (reduce P), then distill gradients again (reduce m further).
- Useful conceptual framing: the paper unifies dataset distillation with tangent-feature subspace selection (Eq. 4) and provides an interpretable one-step bound (Theorem 3.3) and PCA-of-gradient-covariance characterization (Cor. 3.5). The inducing-point/Nyström connection (Eq. 9) helps relate the approach to kernel approximation literature.
- Empirical evidence that per-class NTK matrices on the distilled set have low effective rank (Fig. 2) and that accuracy/fidelity saturate quickly with number of gradients/rank (Figs. 1, 5). The local/global “gap” visualization (Fig. 4) motivates Algorithm 1.
- The gradient synthesis algorithm is reasonably well specified (Algorithm 1) and compared to multiple baselines (random, k-means, leverage, FPS) with gains at extreme compression.

Weaknesses:
- Soundness gaps / unclear guarantees for the full pipeline: the theory mostly justifies components in isolation (distillation-as-subspace, JL preservation, PCA optimality in a relaxed setting). There is no end-to-end theorem connecting (WMDD distillation + JL projection + Algorithm 1 synthesis) to a bound on downstream prediction error of KRR relative to the full NTK on the original dataset. In particular, the “five orders of magnitude” claim is not backed by a rigorous complexity-vs-error tradeoff analysis across all steps.
- Ambiguity about what is being approximated and when: experiments compute kernels on a distilled dataset X~ (size 500) rather than the original dataset; the main claimed benefit of “compressing the data dimension” is therefore not demonstrated as an approximation to the NTK on the full dataset X (n). It is somewhat unclear whether the target is (i) approximating the full NTK on real data, (ii) enabling NTK analysis on a small proxy dataset, or (iii) approximating a model’s predictions on test data.
- Experimental scope is limited: results are shown primarily for ImageNette/ResNet-18, with a smaller extension to ImageWoof. Claims about scaling to O(10^3–10^4) samples and “4–6 orders of magnitude” savings would be more convincing with wall-clock/memory measurements, larger n, and more architectures.
- Algorithm 1 relies on spectral clustering and global eigendecomposition of an m×m kernel (with stated O(n^3) costs). This can be a bottleneck; the paper calls it “one-time,” but for practical NTK analysis workflows, m may need to be much larger than 500. The method’s scalability relative to existing sketching approaches is not empirically validated.
- Some presentation issues: several key empirical claims reference figures/appendices but the core experimental protocol lacks details needed for reproducibility (e.g., exact WMDD settings, projection dimension k choices, how k relates to JL error, hyperparameter selection rules for τv, τg, H beyond grid search). Also, the text sometimes interchanges n/m (original vs distilled sizes), which can confuse complexity statements.

Dimension-specific assessment:
- Soundness: Good overall, but the main pipeline’s end-to-end correctness is not fully established and the experimental target (full-data NTK vs distilled-data NTK) is not always crisply defined.
- Presentation: Good, with helpful definitions and diagrams; however, there are points of ambiguity about objectives/targets and incomplete experimental details.
- Significance: Potentially significant for enabling empirical-NTK-based analyses at larger scale, but demonstrated impact is currently narrow (small-to-mid setting, few datasets/models) and practical scalability of the eigen-based gradient distillation is uncertain.
- Originality: The combination of dataset distillation (to reduce Jacobian evaluations) with NTK computation and the specific local/global spectral gradient synthesis is novel within the framing of NTK approximation; still, pieces (JL, Nyström, coresets) are standard and novelty hinges on the integration and the particular algorithmic instantiation.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) What is the precise approximation target of DNTK: approximating the empirical NTK on the original dataset X (n points), or constructing an NTK/KRR model on a distilled proxy dataset X~? If the former, can you report error metrics between K_XX (or predictions from KRR trained on X) and the distilled/projection/synthesized approximation?

2) Theoretical: can you provide an end-to-end bound (even informal, with clearly stated assumptions) connecting (i) input distillation size m, (ii) JL dimension k, and (iii) gradient synthesis size s to a bound on (a) kernel matrix error ||K − K̂|| (spectral/Frobenius) and/or (b) prediction error of KRR? Right now the guarantees appear componentwise.

3) Complexity/claims: where exactly do the “4–6 orders of magnitude” and “up to five orders” reductions come from in your experiments? Please provide concrete wall-clock time and memory numbers for: full gradients on real data (or largest feasible baseline), distillation-only, distillation+JL, and full DNTK (including Algorithm 1 costs).

4) Algorithm 1 scalability: since it uses spectral clustering and eigen/SVD on an m×m matrix, how does performance and runtime behave for m in the 10^4 range (which the conclusion suggests)? Are there approximations (e.g., randomized eigensolvers) and do they preserve the local/global gap behavior?

5) Evaluation protocol: when reporting “fidelity,” are you comparing KRR predictions to the base network on the same test distribution, and are the labels Y used in KRR always the base network logits (as per Appendix B), or sometimes ground-truth labels? How sensitive are results to this choice?
review.limitations:
The paper includes a brief impact statement claiming no serious risks, but it does not substantively discuss limitations or negative societal impacts.

Suggestions: (i) clarify that improved NTK approximations could be used for model auditing and shift detection, but also could lower the cost of certain surveillance/classification deployments; (ii) discuss limitations around the lazy-regime assumption, dependence on pretrained features and WMDD quality, and scalability bottlenecks of eigen-based gradient distillation; (iii) address potential failure cases (e.g., tasks where NTK spectra are not low-rank, or where distillation alters the tangent space relevant to real data).

title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

review.summary:
The paper studies stochastic black-box optimization of an unknown L-Lipschitz function over a compact domain (primarily [0,1]^d) with sub-Gaussian noise, targeting PAC-style simple-regret guarantees. It introduces Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP), which maintains an explicit “active set” A_t of potentially optimal points defined by a confidence-adjusted Lipschitz upper envelope U_t(x)=min_i (UCB_i(t)+L d(x,x_i)) and a global lower certificate \ell_t=max_i LCB_i(t); the active set is A_t={x: U_t(x)\ge \ell_t}. Points outside A_t are declared certifiably suboptimal with high probability, and the paper proposes using the shrinking of A_t (and its volume) as an anytime progress/stopping signal. 

Theoretical contributions include (i) containment and shrinkage results linking A_t to a near-optimal set under a margin/near-optimality-dimension condition (Assumption 2.3), yielding a volume bound Vol(A_t)\le C(2(\beta_t+L\eta_t)+\gamma_t)^{d-\alpha}, and (ii) a sample-complexity upper bound \tilde O(L^d \varepsilon^{-(2+\alpha)}) along with a matching lower bound \Omega(\varepsilon^{-(2+\alpha)}). 

Algorithmic extensions are: CGP-Adaptive, which learns an unknown Lipschitz constant by detecting Lipschitz violations and doubling \hat L, with an O(log(L*/\hat L_0)) overhead; CGP-TR, a trust-region variant with “certified restarts” that provides local certificates and is intended to scale to d up to 100; and CGP-Hybrid, which uses CGP to certify/prune then optionally switches to GP-UCB within A_t when a heuristic local-smoothness ratio \rho is small. Experiments on 12 benchmarks (2D–100D) compare several baselines and report regret, certificate-based early stopping, and runtime comparisons.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The core certificate definition (A_t via U_t and \ell_t) is clear and yields a straightforward correctness argument on the stated “good event” (Lemmas 4.1–4.3, Theorem 4.5). The shrinkage theorem (Theorem 4.6) cleanly connects the active set to the margin/near-optimality-dimension assumption and provides an interpretable decomposition in terms of confidence radius \beta_t, covering radius \eta_t, and lower-bound gap proxy \gamma_t. The paper also explicitly separates certificate validity from approximate volume estimation (Remark 4.7), which is important.
- Weaknesses / concerns: Several critical algorithmic components that affect the theoretical quantities are only described heuristically and are not fully reconciled with the assumptions used to prove the rates.
  1) The theory assumes oracle access to argmax over A_t of a non-smooth score, but the implementation uses CMA-ES with restarts; the paper states this “may slow convergence of \eta_t but does not invalidate certificates,” which is plausible for validity but leaves the sample-complexity proof depending on how \eta_t is ensured to decrease. Theorem 4.8’s derivation uses an explicit covering-number argument that presumes an achieved covering radius; the algorithmic mechanism guaranteeing \eta_t=O(\varepsilon/L) within the stated sample budget is not formally proved.
  2) CGP-Adaptive’s certificates are explicitly not anytime-valid when starting from \hat L_0<L* (Remark 5.2, Theorem 5.1(4)), which undermines one of the central motivations (“anytime certificates”) unless the user already has a safe overestimate. This is acknowledged, but it raises questions about practical certificate use in the unknown-L setting.
  3) The lower bound (Theorem 4.9) is presented as a proof sketch with several steps (e.g., Fano-based argument and per-cell sample requirement) that are not fully formalized in the paper text; it may be correct in spirit, but it is hard to verify without a more precise construction (especially how Assumption 2.3 is met with the chosen M=\varepsilon^{-\alpha} partition and how the KL terms are bounded under the sampling model).
  4) The CGP-TR guarantees (Theorem 6.1) rely on conditions like “a trust region containing x* is not contracted to exclude x*” and a diameter condition L·diam(T_j)\le \Delta_j/8 “eventually bounded”; these are nontrivial and depend on the trust-region adaptation scheme, but the paper does not fully specify assumptions ensuring they hold.

Presentation:
- Strengths: The paper is generally well organized: problem setup, algorithm, core theory, then extensions and experiments. Definitions of U_t, \ell_t, A_t are crisp, and the certificate interpretation is intuitive. Tables/figures (e.g., Table 1, Figure 1, Table 7) directly support the “certificate utility” narrative.
- Weaknesses: Some claims are stated more strongly than what is proven in the main text. For example, CGP-Hybrid’s Proposition 7.1(2) essentially defers any rate to empirical behavior and mentions GP information gain without providing a concrete guarantee; yet the surrounding text sometimes frames hybrid as “best of both worlds” in a way that could be read as more principled than it is. Also, the experiments repeatedly reference tables (e.g., “Table 6 shows … wins on all 12 benchmarks”) but the full 12-benchmark table is not shown in the provided excerpt (only partial tables), making it harder to assess completeness.

Significance:
- Strengths: Exporting an explicit, computable certificate/active set (and corresponding stopping criteria) is a practically meaningful contribution for “precious call” optimization, beyond just regret bounds. The local-certificate idea in trust regions is also potentially impactful for bringing Lipschitz-style guarantees to higher dimensions.
- Weaknesses: The practical significance depends on whether the certificate computations (membership, volume estimation, or estimating \eta_t) are tractable and reliable in the intended regimes (d up to 100), and whether certificates remain meaningful under unknown L and approximate maximization. The paper claims tractability via Monte Carlo/nested-set estimators and local certificates, but the overhead and robustness of these certificate-related computations are not deeply validated beyond summary runtime tables.

Originality:
- Strengths: The central framing—making pruning/certification an explicit, user-facing object (A_t, Vol(A_t), gap proxy) rather than an implicit artifact of zooming/tree analyses—is a clear conceptual shift. The certified restart condition in CGP-TR is also a neat and simple safety mechanism that leverages the certificate.
- Weaknesses: The mathematical ingredients (UCB + Lipschitz envelope + near-optimality dimension rates) are closely aligned with known optimistic Lipschitz/zooming analyses, and some contributions are primarily packaging/engineering rather than new theory. That said, the certificate-centric framing and the modular hybridization are reasonably novel within the paper’s own positioning.

Overall, I view the paper as promising and conceptually clean, with strong motivation and decent empirical evidence, but with notable gaps between the algorithm as implemented (approximate maximization, trust-region adaptation, unknown-L regime) and the precise conditions needed for the claimed end-to-end sample-complexity guarantees.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Theorem 4.8 depends on driving the covering radius \eta_t to O(\varepsilon/L). What property of the CGP query rule (argmax of score within A_t) ensures \eta_t decreases at the rate implicitly used in the covering-number argument? Can you provide a formal lemma connecting the selection rule (with \lambda=L) to a bound on \eta_t as a function of the number of distinct sampled locations?

2) In CGP-Adaptive with \hat L_0<L*, certificates are invalid before the final doubling. In your experiments and in the proposed “principled stopping,” do you only stop after reaching \hat L\ge L* (i.e., after no violations for some time), or do you sometimes stop earlier? If earlier, what safety guarantee (if any) is provided to users?

3) For CGP-TR, Theorem 6.1 assumes a trust region containing x* is “not contracted to exclude x*” (e.g., fixed center and r_min). In the actual implementation, how are centers updated (if at all), and can contraction/expansion steps ever move or clip regions such that x* might be excluded even without a certified restart? Please clarify the exact trust-region mechanics used in experiments.

4) Volume estimation for d>5 uses subset simulation with hit-and-run sampling. How sensitive are the reported stopping rules and shrinkage-validation plots to mixing issues / estimator variance when Vol(A_t) becomes very small? Do you have diagnostics (e.g., effective sample size, multiple chains) demonstrating the estimator is reliable in the hardest (d=60/100) settings?

5) The lower bound (Theorem 4.9) is given as a sketch. Can you provide a complete argument (in the appendix) that explicitly verifies Assumption 2.3 with the constructed family and derives the \Omega(\varepsilon^{-(2+\alpha)}) bound under the stated sub-Gaussian noise model and adaptive sampling?
review.limitations: Partially. The paper explicitly notes core limitations (needs Lipschitz continuity; vanilla CGP limited to moderate d; CGP-TR offers local not global certificates) and includes an Impact Statement warning about Lipschitz violations. However, it would be helpful to (i) more prominently emphasize that CGP-Adaptive may produce invalid certificates during the learning phase unless initialized with a conservative overestimate, and (ii) discuss potential failure modes from approximate maximization and approximate volume estimation (particularly how users should interpret certificates/progress signals when these approximations are poor). On societal impacts, the statement is reasonable but could add discussion of risks in safety-critical settings if Lipschitz assumptions are violated or if certificates are misunderstood as absolute guarantees under model mismatch.

title: Embedding Morphology into Transformers for Cross-Robot Policy Learning

review.summary: The paper proposes an embodiment-aware modification to a Transformer-based vision-language-action (VLA) policy (built on a π0.5-style backbone) to improve cross-robot and within-robot performance by explicitly injecting robot morphology. The method introduces (i) kinematic tokens: per-joint action representations formed by temporally chunking each joint’s action trajectory and embedding these joint-wise vectors as additional tokens; (ii) topology-aware attention bias applied specifically to joint-to-joint attention among kinematic tokens, implemented via hard masking (Full-Mask or alternating Mix-Mask) or a soft shortest-path-distance (SPD) bias; and (iii) joint-attribute conditioning using FiLM to modulate kinematic-token embeddings based on per-joint descriptors (joint type, axis, limits, contact-related parameters). Experiments in simulation evaluate single-embodiment imitation learning on DROID (Franka Panda) and Unitree G1 Dex1, plus a multi-embodiment joint-training setting on Panda+SO101, with ablations over masking choices, temporal chunk size, auxiliary kinematic tokens, and soft-mask initialization.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The architectural interventions are clearly defined (token construction, where topology bias is applied, FiLM conditioning). The evaluation includes component-wise ablations (KT vs. masks vs. FiLM), comparisons across multiple topology bias variants (Full/Mix/Soft), and some sensitivity checks (chunk size, auxiliary tokens, bias initialization for Soft-Mask). Uncertainty is quantified with 95% CIs over 300 rollouts per condition.
- Weaknesses: The “cross-robot” claim is only partially supported by the multi-embodiment experiment: it trains and evaluates on the same two embodiments (Panda+SO101) rather than testing transfer to a held-out embodiment, and it uses an imbalanced mixture ratio (80/20) that likely biases improvements toward Panda (as acknowledged in Appendix F). Also, training protocols differ across benchmarks (AP-FT vs Full-FT, different model scale), which makes it harder to attribute gains purely to morphology encoding vs. optimization/budget differences. For multi-embodiment, only learning curves are shown; there is no final table with per-embodiment, per-task SR with CIs at convergence, nor statistical tests of differences at the end.

Presentation:
- Strengths: Method is communicated with intuitive figures and explicit equations; the mask placement is clarified with an attention-mask diagram. Tables are readable and report CIs. The paper anticipates common questions by including soft-mask stability exploration and initialization ablations.
- Weaknesses: Some naming/notation is mildly confusing (G used both as number of temporal chunks and as the kinematic graph symbol in different sections). The relationship between “action tokens” in π0.5 and the introduced kinematic tokens could be explained more concretely (e.g., exact token counts/positions, and whether kinematic tokens are derived from ground-truth actions during training and from predicted actions during inference or only used as latent context). Multi-embodiment evaluation details for SO101 are relatively light (task suite specifics, number of tasks, and exact SR definition per environment are not tabulated in the main text).

Significance:
- Strengths: If robust, the result that explicit morphology tokens + topology bias + joint descriptors substantially improve success rate even in single-embodiment imitation learning (e.g., DROID sim-evals) suggests morphology is a meaningful inductive bias for VLA-style action generation, not only for explicit multi-robot settings. The approach is lightweight and seems compatible with existing transformer policies via token/interface design.
- Weaknesses: The demonstrated multi-embodiment gains are modest and mixed (Macro SR improves in the curve, but Appendix F indicates SO101 may be slightly worse at the end). Without held-out-embodiment generalization or broader task diversity, it is unclear how much this advances “cross-robot policy learning” beyond improving a particular fine-tuning setup.

Originality:
- Strengths: The key novelty is the “kinematic token” interface that converts joint-space actions into per-joint tokens compatible with topology-aware attention within a VLA policy, plus combining it with a local/global masking schedule and explicit joint-attribute FiLM conditioning.
- Weaknesses: Topology-aware attention and FiLM-style conditioning are established mechanisms; the paper’s novelty is mainly in the integration and interface design rather than a fundamentally new learning objective or theoretical insight. Still, the integration appears nontrivial and empirically motivated.

Empirical strengths/weaknesses (additional):
- DROID: Large improvement over baseline on average SR (19.7% → 47.4% with KT+Mix-Mask+FiLM), but the per-task breakdown shows Task 1 can drop severely for some variants (e.g., best overall has 5.7% on Task 1), raising questions about task trade-offs and whether macro averages hide regressions.
- Unitree G1 Dex1: Gains are small (24.7% → 28.0%) and KT alone does not help; improvements come mainly from Mix-Mask and FiLM, suggesting the effect may depend on embodiment/task.
- Reproducibility: Hyperparameters are summarized, and ablations are extensive, but details like random seed counts for training runs (vs just rollout randomization), dataset sizes for each benchmark subset, and whether results are averaged over multiple training seeds are not clear.
review.key_questions_for_authors:
1) Kinematic tokens: during training/inference, what exactly are the kinematic tokens computed from? Are they embedded from ground-truth action sequences (teacher forcing) and only serve as additional context, and if so, what replaces them at inference time when actions are unknown? If they are derived from predicted actions, how is this bootstrapped without circularity?
2) Multi-embodiment setting: can you provide final per-embodiment (Panda and SO101) success rates with 95% CIs at the end of training (e.g., 125k), and ideally per-task breakdown for Panda’s 3 tasks, to assess whether Macro SR improvements come from one robot while the other regresses?
3) Training stability / variance: are the reported numbers from a single training run per condition or averaged over multiple training seeds? If single-run, how sensitive are the main gains (e.g., 19.7%→47.4% on DROID) to training seed?
4) Action-space mismatch handling: in the Panda+SO101 joint training, how are action dimensions aligned in the shared policy (padding, masking, separate heads, or fixed max-J with per-embodiment joint masks)? How does topology masking interact with “missing” joints?
5) Joint descriptors: are the per-joint attributes always available and accurate across all embodiments and simulators? Did you test robustness to missing/incorrect descriptors, or a reduced descriptor set, to show which semantic features drive the FiLM gains?
review.limitations: No. The impact statement discusses broad societal implications (automation/labor) but the limitations discussion is not sufficiently concrete about methodological and evaluation limits. Suggestions: explicitly acknowledge that “cross-robot” evaluation is not held-out-embodiment generalization; discuss potential reliance on simulator-provided joint/contact parameters for FiLM (availability on real robots, sim-to-real discrepancies); analyze task trade-offs/regressions (e.g., DROID Task 1 drops in best model) and when morphology biases may hurt; and mention computational/latency costs due to added tokens (especially with auxiliary kinematic tokens) and how this scales with higher-DoF robots.

title: ALIEN: Analytic Latent Watermarking for Controllable Generation

review.summary: The paper proposes ALIEN, a training-light semantic watermarking framework for latent diffusion models that embeds a message by injecting an analytically derived, time-dependent correction into the U-Net noise prediction during sampling. ALIEN has two stages: (i) training a secret encoder/decoder to map a message to a latent residual δ_w that can be decoded from the final latent, and (ii) enforcing a z0-space watermark constraint by deriving (under a VP-SDE formulation) the required reverse-drift correction and translating it into a closed-form modulation term added at each denoising step. The method is presented as sampler-agnostic (including irreversible samplers) and instantiated in two configurations, ALIEN-Q (quality-oriented) and ALIEN-R (robustness-oriented), differing mainly in injection window and strength. Experiments on Stable Diffusion v1.5/v2.1 compare against post-processing, latent modification, constrained sampling, optimization-based, and model fine-tuning baselines, reporting improvements in visual quality, stability across samplers/hyperparameters, robustness under various attacks (including regenerative and VAE-based), and substantial efficiency gains over optimization-based approaches.
review.strengths_and_weaknesses:
Soundness:
- Strengths: The core idea is clean and technically motivated: impose a z0 constraint and derive the necessary score shift and reverse-drift correction in a VP-SDE view, yielding a closed-form coefficient for injecting δ_w via noise prediction modulation. The appendix provides a derivation chain (constraint → Tweedie/score relation → drift correction → noise offset), and the resulting algorithm is straightforward.
- Weaknesses: Several key technical assumptions/links are under-specified, limiting full confidence in the “first analytic derivation” and sampler-agnostic claims.
